zh:
“瞧,那老头又来了！”演武场外，朱漆门隙间漏出两点寒甲幽光，新戍卫阿景与阿达正在暗处窃窃私语。
“自这疯督军来后，咱们操练得比狗都勤。” 阿景撇撇嘴，将腰间蹀躞带晃得叮当响。
彼时，他们窥视的老人正凝望演武场西侧人墙。
三日前此人突兀出现在禁军营口，神情恍惚，疯疯癫癫。穿着破旧铠甲，手持一褪色古卷，腰上还悬一柄锈迹斑驳的横刀，刀鞘的刻字已经模糊难辩了。当值士卒记得，这疯子抚着辕门石兽突然恸哭：“尔等竟连十斤角弓都开不得吗——若敌军袭来，如何守得住啊！”
军士们一时不知如何是好，便绑了着这蓬头老翁到将军营帐前。那疯癫老者褴褛衣袍下筋肉虬结，脊梁似戟，只一双眼混沌。
“护送…人…财...”老翁突然嘶吼，惊得士卒纷纷拔刀。然而或是这老翁命不该绝，此夜正巧府尹也在营中与将军相谈。府尹见状喝止众人，细细看了老翁一会儿，突然起身让众士卒退下。几日后，办起了操练会。
“诶诶诶，我听大索说，那日他亲眼看到府尹大人摸了那老疯子的刀！你说，他是不是大人的亲戚啊？”阿景捅了捅阿达。
“嘶，样貌嘛，不大像。”阿达挠挠头。
“啧，不是亲戚，大人护着他干啥？难道……”阿景一脸狡黠。而后突然想到了什么，眼睛一亮。
“要不，咱去找他‘取取经’吧？看他到底靠啥得了大人青眼，咱也学学，到时加官进爵……”
“不行！”阿达泼了盆冷水。
“讨了大人欢心，说不得能娶贵女...”阿景压低嗓子，继续劝说。
“险！”阿达后撤半步。
“当百夫长！”
“悬！”
“少值夜...”
阿达挣扎半刻后，仿佛下了极大决心。
“…试试。”
“走吧兄弟！”
en:
"Look, that old man's here again!" Outside the Training Ground, two glints of cold armor leaked through the crack of the vermilion-lacquered gate. The new guards, Jing and Da, were whispering in the shadows.
"Ever since this mad military governor showed up, we've been training harder than mules," Jing muttered.
At that moment, the old man they were spying on was gazing fixedly at the bulwark on the western side of the Training Ground.

Three days ago, this man had abruptly appeared at the entrance of the Imperial Guards' camp, dazed and seemingly mad. He wore tattered armor, clutched a faded ancient scroll, and had a rust-spotted Heng Blade hanging at his waist, its scabbard's engraving worn beyond recognition. The soldiers on duty remembered the madman suddenly breaking down in tears while stroking the stone beast at the camp gate: "Can you truly not even draw a ten-jin hornbow?! How will you hold fast if the enemy attacks?!"
The guards, unsure what to do, had tied up the disheveled old man and brought him before the general's tent. Beneath his ragged robes, the mad old man's muscles were knotted like cords, his spine straight as a spear, but his eyes were clouded.
"Escort... the people... the treasure..." the old man suddenly roared, startling the soldiers into drawing their blades. Yet perhaps fate decreed the old man should live, for that very night the Prefect happened to be in the camp, conferring with the general. Seeing the commotion, the Prefect halted the men, studied the old man closely for a moment, then suddenly rose and ordered the soldiers to withdraw. A few days later, intensive training drills began.

"Hey, hey, I heard from Big Suo that he saw it with his own eyes that day—the Prefect touched that old madman's sword! Is he a relative of the Prefect?" Jing nudged Da.
"Hiss... their looks don't quite match," Da scratched his head.
"Tsk, if not a relative, why would the Prefect protect him? Unless..." Jing's face turned sly. Then, as if struck by a thought, his eyes lit up.
"How about we go to him for some 'advice'? See what he did to earn the Prefect's favor, learn from it, then promotions wait for us..."
"No way!" Da poured cold water on the idea.
"With the Prefect's favor, we may even marry his daughter..." Jing lowered his voice, pressing on.
"Too risky!" Da took half a step back.
"Become a centurion!"
"Unlikely!"
"Fewer night watches..."
After a moment's struggle, Da seemed to steel himself with great resolve. "...We can try."
"Let's go, bro!"
DravenEcho

zh:
阿景推搡着阿达蹭到堆人墙的赛场边时，张叔正用枯指虚虚勾绘着人墙，残甲缝隙里渗出晨光。
“张叔？”阿景靴尖碾着砂石。
张叔只是沉沉地看着人墙："该垒七丈...该..."
阿达解下新得的牛皮水囊递过去："您老可是认识咱府尹大人？"
张叔依旧不理人，摩挲着胸口残甲。
二人对视了一眼，阿景肘击同伴肋下，豁出去般扯嗓子嚷：“老将军！"
张叔猛然转身，浑浊瞳仁里泛起光彩："归...归..."
话音未落，腿影扫来。两个少年栽进人墙堆中时，听见后方炸雷般的吼声：“去，去上面！“
两个少年面面相觑，当即想逃。但张叔盯着他们不说，围观侠民的哄笑裹着枣木梆子声涌来。无法，为了不丢面儿，二人只得在众人的“注目礼”中，硬着头皮往上爬。
阿景的靴子刚踩上第三层人桩的膝盖窝，底下立即传来闷哼："龟儿子……踩你爷爷……"
阿达拽着不知是谁的衣裳借力，突然凌空飞来一巴掌，打的他发蒙——搭作第七层的两个老兵正抓着自己的裤腰带，用看死人的眼神盯着他们。
当阿达的鼻梁第七次撞上别人的护心镜时，头顶忽传来沙哑的欢呼："到顶！到顶！”
他们终于稳稳地站在了人墙顶上。
张叔仰起的下颌，凝望着人墙，口中念叨。
“归家……归家……这么高……能看到家吗？”
而后，便蹒跚着离开了，两个少年呆愣着看张叔走远。
“诶诶……”阿达急切探身欲喊，整面人墙应声坍作满地烟尘。
“追！”阿景吐出嘴里的草屑，瘸着腿追向烟尘里那道佝偻背影。
en:
Jing pushed and shoved Da as they edged toward the crowd gathered around the bulwark competition. Uncle Zhang was using withered fingers to trace the shape of the bulwark in the air, morning light seeping through the gaps in his broken armor. 
"Uncle Zhang?" Jing's boot scuffed the gravel. 
Uncle Zhang merely stared heavily at the bulwark. "Should be seven zhang high... should..."
Da took off his newly acquired cowhide waterskin and offered it. "Sir, do you know our Prefect?" 
Uncle Zhang still ignored them, stroking the broken armor on his chest. 
The two exchanged a glance. Jing elbowed his companion in the ribs and, as if casting caution to the wind, shouted, "Old General!" 
Uncle Zhang whirled around. A gleam flickered in his clouded eyes. "Return... return..."
Before he could finish, a leg swept out. As the two youths tumbled into the heap of the bulwark, they heard a thunderous roar behind them. "Go! Get to the top!" They looked at each other, wanting nothing more than to flee. But Uncle Zhang was watching them, and the jeers and laughter of the watching townsfolk, mingled with the clacking of jujube wood clappers, washed over them. With no choice and not wanting to lose face, they gritted their teeth and began to climb under the crowd's "watchful gaze." 
No sooner had Jing's boot stepped onto the knee hollow of the third layer of bodies than a muffled groan came from below. "You dog... stepping on your granddad..."
Da, pulling himself up by someone's clothing, was suddenly slapped out of the blue, leaving him dazed—two veterans forming the seventh layer were gripping their own belts, staring at them as if they were dead men. 
When Da's nose bridge collided with someone's breastplate for the seventh time, a hoarse cheer suddenly came from above. "The top! You've reached the top!" 
They finally stood steadily atop the bulwark. 
Uncle Zhang lifted his chin, gazing at the bulwark, muttering to himself. 
"Going home... going home... this high... can we see home from here?" 
Then, he shuffled away. The two youths stared dumbfounded as Uncle Zhang walked off. 
"Hey, hey..." Da leaned forward urgently, about to call out, when the entire bulwark collapsed into a cloud of dust. 
"After him!" Jing spat out the grass in his mouth and limped after the stooped figure disappearing into the dust.

后郭威屠城时，此法随九流门弟子散落城外，又被逃亡的老鼠叼走藏于洞穴……
若干年后，该鼠举家搬迁至琼林苑时，被巡游木鸢抓住，而心法，也随之落入木鸢腹中。
en:
Ni Laoshan was brave and journeyed a lot on his own. 
One day, he fell into the water after being seriously injured, and saw several fish swim by. 
Between life and death, he was enlightened. Fish use the water to travel, and cranes use the wind to fly. When walking the Jianghu, one should rely on power. That was why he created the Inner Way. 
When Guo Wei devastated the city, the art left the city with disciples of Nine Mortal Ways, then was picked up by a fleeting mouse and hidden in a cave. 
Many years later, when the mouse moved with its family to Jadewood Court, they were caught by a patrolling wooden eagle, and the Inner Ways ended up inside the wooden eagle.

zh: 唯有其中一种，赤瞳蓝羽，时凫水，时盘旋，时畏缩如枣核，时伸颈如玉瓶，形状百种，五分深沉，三分畏缩，二分似偷儿，十分可笑。易与其他禽类混同，不知其本名。问画者，答曰：夜鹭。古来诗赋多有鸿鹄乌鹊之属，故识者多。而未闻有夜鹭诗赋者，故名声不显。惜哉。夜鹭百态，观一鸟如同观百鸟，百年之后，必有贤人作夜鹭诗赋。
en: Yet, there is one creature that defies such easy grace: a bird with striking crimson eyes and slate-blue plumage. Sometimes it drifts aimlessly upon the ripples; sometimes it spirals awkwardly through the sky. One moment, it shrinks into itself, curling up as tight as a little date pit; the next, it stretches its neck as long and slender as a jade vase. Its postures are entirely unpredictable. It looks five parts solemn, three parts terrified, and two parts petty thief in the night, making it utterly, wonderfully absurd. Easily mistaken for its more elegant cousins, I never knew its true name until I asked the local artists, who called it the night heron. Ancient poetry endlessly extols the swan and the magpie, crowning them with literary immortality. Yet, I have never once read an ode or a poem dedicated to the night heron. What a profound pity. This bird possesses a hundred different guises; to watch a single night heron is to watch a hundred different birds at play. I am certain that a century from now, a wise and perceptive poet will finally come along to immortalize it in verse.

zh:
寒香寻在江湖上混迹多年，自诩见过不少奇人怪人，可像这样带个孩子浪迹天涯的人自己还真是第一次见。

“喂，我说你这人，自己过这刀口舔血的日子也就罢了，带个孩子出来算是怎么个事？莫不是欠下什么风流债，人家把孩子丢给了你？”
“孩子是捡的。”
“……，你倒是热心。”
“没爹没娘的，天下大雨，我捡是不捡？”

寒香寻没再接话，可目光还是忍不住往他那儿飘去，见这人也不哄孩子，真不像亲生的。
远处追兵的声音更近了。寒香寻思索片刻还是没忍住，咒骂着将身上的蝉翼甲丢给了江无浪。
“先说好，我是看这孩子可怜，可不是怕你死了！”

“多谢。”江无浪挥刀解决了一个从寒香寻身后而来的追兵，接着将蝉翼甲裹在了孩子的身上。
en:
Han Xiangxun has roamed the jianghu for years and prided herself on having met all kinds of odd and unforgettable souls, but never has she seen someone traveling the world with a child in arms.

"Hey you! Living on the edge, risking your neck? Fine, that's your business. But what's with dragging a kid along? Some lover dumped the kid on you or something?"
"The kid's adopted."
"... Well. That's unexpectedly soft-hearted of you."
"No family, no home. It was pouring. What else was I supposed to do? Leave the kid there?"

Han Xiangxun didn't reply, but her eyes lingered on him. He didn't so much as pat the child's back, didn't offer a word of comfort. He didn't look like a father at all.
The sound of approaching enemies began to echo from down the path. After a brief pause, she clicked her tongue, muttered a curse, and hurled her cicada wing pendant toward him.
"Let's be clear. I'm doing this for the kid, not because I care if you make it out alive."

"Thank you," Jiang Wulang said, already turning to slash down an enemy emerging from the trees behind her. In one fluid motion, he wrapped the pendant around the child.

zh:
【觐礼第十】

觐礼。至于郊，王使人皮弁用璧劳。侯氏亦皮弁迎于帷门之外，再拜。使者不答拜，遂执玉，三揖。至于阶，使者不让，先升。侯氏升听命，降，再拜稽首，遂升受玉。使者左还而立，侯氏还璧，使者受。侯氏降，再拜稽首，使者乃出。侯氏及止使者，使者乃入。侯氏与之让升。侯氏先升，授几。侯氏拜送几；使者设几，答拜。侯氏用束帛、乘马傧使者，使者再拜受。侯氏再拜送币。使者降，以左骖出。侯氏送于门外，再拜。侯氏遂从之。
天子赐舍，曰：“伯父，女顺命于王所，赐伯父舍！”侯氏再拜稽首，傧之束帛、乘马。
天子使大夫戒，曰：“某日，伯父帅乃初事。”侯氏再拜稽首。
诸侯前朝，皆受舍于朝。同姓西面北上，异姓东面北上。
侯氏裨冕，释币于祢。乘墨车，载龙旂、弧韣乃朝以瑞玉，有缫。
天子设斧依于户牖之间，左右几。天子衮冕，负斧依。啬夫承命，告于天子。天子曰：“非他，伯父实来，予一人嘉之。伯父其入，予一人将受之。”侯氏入门右，坐奠圭，再拜稽首。摈者谒。侯氏坐取圭，升致命。王受之玉。侯氏降，阶东北面再拜稽首。摈者延之，曰：“升！”升成拜，乃出。
四享皆束帛加璧，庭实唯国所有。奉束帛，匹马卓上，九马随之，中庭西上，奠币，再拜稽首。摈者曰：“予一人将受之。”侯氏升，致命。王抚玉。侯氏降自西阶，东面授宰币，西阶前再拜稽首，以马出，授人，九马随之。事毕。
乃右肉袒于庙门之东。乃入门右，北面立，告听事。摈者谒诸天子。天子辞于侯氏，曰：“伯父无事，归宁乃邦！”侯氏再拜稽首，出，自屏南适门西，遂入门左，北面立，王劳之。再拜稽首。摈者延之，曰：“升！”升成拜，降出。
天子赐侯氏以车服。迎于外门外，再拜。路先设，西上，路下四，亚之，重赐无数，在车南。诸公奉箧服，加命书于其上，升自西阶，东面，大史是右。侯氏升，西面立。大史述命。侯氏降两阶之间；北面再拜稽首，升成拜。大史加书于服上，侯氏受。使者出。侯氏送，再拜，傧使者，诸公赐服者，束帛、四马，傧大史亦如之。
……
en:
【Chapter 10: The Audience Rite】

The Audience Rite. When the marquis arrives at the outskirts, the king sends an envoy wearing a leather cap to greet him with a jade disc. The marquis, also in a leather cap, welcomes him outside the curtained gate, bowing twice. The envoy does not return the bow but takes the jade and makes three salutations. Arriving at the steps, the envoy, without yielding, ascends first. The marquis ascends to receive the command, descends, bows twice and knocks his head, then ascends to receive the jade. The envoy turns left and stands; the marquis returns the jade, and the envoy receives it. The marquis descends, bows twice and knocks his head, and the envoy then departs. The marquis stops the envoy, who then re-enters. The marquis yields to the envoy in ascending. The marquis ascends first and presents the armrest. The marquis bows while presenting the armrest; the envoy sets it down and returns the bow. The marquis entertains the envoy with a bolt of silk and a team of four horses; the envoy bows twice and receives them. The marquis bows twice in sending off the gifts. The envoy descends and leaves by the left trace horse. The marquis sees him off outside the gate, bowing twice, and then follows him.
The Emperor grants a residence, saying: "Uncle, you have obeyed the command at the king's court; I grant you this residence!" The marquis bows twice and knocks his head, and entertains the envoy with a bolt of silk and a team of four horses.
The Emperor sends a high official to announce: "On such a day, Uncle, you shall begin your duties." The marquis bows twice and knocks his head.
Before the audience, all the lords receive their lodgings at the court. Those of the same surname face west, ranked from the north; those of different surnames face east, ranked from the north.
The marquis, in ceremonial robes and cap, offers silk at the ancestral shrine. Riding in a black carriage, bearing the dragon banner and the bow case, he comes to the audience with the auspicious jade, which is set on a mat.
The Emperor sets up the axe-embroidered screen between the door and the window, with armrests on left and right. The Emperor, in his dragon robe and cap, stands with his back to the screen. The steward receives the command and reports to the Emperor. The Emperor says: "It is no other; Uncle has indeed come, and I commend him. Let Uncle enter; I shall receive him." The marquis enters by the right of the gate, kneels to place the gui jade, bows twice and knocks his head. The usher announces him. The marquis kneels to pick up the jade, ascends to deliver his message. The king receives the jade. The marquis descends, and at the east of the steps, facing north, bows twice and knocks his head. The usher invites him, saying: "Ascend!" He ascends, completes the bow, and then departs.
At the four presentations, all include a bolt of silk with a jade disc added, and the courtyard offerings are whatever the state possesses. He presents the bolt of silk, with one horse leading and nine horses following, arranged in the middle of the courtyard facing west; he places the offerings, bows twice and knocks his head. The usher says: "I shall receive them." The marquis ascends and delivers his message. The king touches the jade. The marquis descends by the western steps, faces east to hand the offerings to the steward, bows twice and knocks his head before the western steps, and leads the horses out to hand them to attendants, with the nine horses following. The ceremony concludes.
Then, baring his right arm at the east of the temple gate, he enters by the right, stands facing north, and announces that he awaits commands. The usher reports to the Emperor. The Emperor declines, saying to the marquis: "Uncle, there is no matter; return to your state and enjoy peace!" The marquis bows twice and knocks his head, departs, and from the south of the screen goes to the west of the gate, then enters by the left, stands facing north, and the king offers him consolation. He bows twice and knocks his head. The usher invites him, saying: "Ascend!" He ascends, completes the bow, descends, and departs.
The Emperor bestows upon the marquis a carriage and robes. He welcomes them outside the outer gate, bowing twice. The road carriage is set out first, facing west; the four horses beneath it follow in order, with additional gifts beyond count placed south of the carriage. The dukes present a chest of robes, placing the decree upon it, ascending by the western steps, facing east, with the Grand Scribe to the right. The marquis ascends and stands facing west. The Grand Scribe recites the decree. The marquis descends between the two sets of steps; facing north, he bows twice and knocks his head, then ascends to complete the bow. The Grand Scribe places the decree upon the robes, and the marquis receives them. The envoy departs. The marquis sees him off, bowing twice, and entertains the envoy; for the dukes who presented the robes, he offers a bolt of silk and four horses, and entertains the Grand Scribe in the same manner.
……

文元言，此地偏险，访客稀少，正是可偷得浮生闲的一隅。
武元言，此地临风，风景极佳，栈道攀援亦可强身健体。

Some once suggested the Twin Mavens relocate closer to the bustling heart of the Archives, but both the Laureate and the Champion politely declined.
The Laureate remarked that the remote, rugged path kept visitors few, making it a perfect haven to steal a moment of peace from worldly hustle.
The Champion held that the breezy summit offered unrivaled views, and the arduous climb served as fine physical training.
Their disciples, however, claim the winding planks and sheer precipices serve as a true test: only those of sincere heart may reach the door.

有，当然有：#Y【月儿升，月儿沉，我家有个聚宝盆。】听罢，小八抬头望天，点了点他的铜脑壳。#E
你将歌谣唱了出来，小八摇晃起了他的铜脑壳，沉醉其中。
“太太太太好听了！”待你唱完，小八不禁发出了感慨。
如此美妙的音乐，当然要用在改造后的八音盒上。
不久之后，小八邀请你来欣赏他的最新大作！
这回，他把八音盒嵌进了火箭中，又把火箭绑在了自己身上。
继“一飞冲天”后，小八的最最新发明——“飞唱不可”再次响彻山中。
——祝小八再次顺利降落！
en:
After just a few days apart, Xiaoba has already dreamed up another new mechanism, which is meant to send music beyond the borders of Mirkvale. But he has run into a problem: what tune should it play? No one in Mirkvale has ever traveled far, so he comes to you for help. "You've been to so many places," he says. "Have you ever heard a melody, one so beautiful, so unforgettable, that it lingers in your heart forever?"
Yes, of course: #Y[The moon will rise, the moon will set... I have a treasure basin.] When he hears it, Xiaoba looks up and nods his little bronze head.#E
You begin to sing, and Xiaoba's little bronze head starts swaying gently from side to side, utterly lost in the music.
"It's so, so, so, so beautiful!" he blurts out the moment you finish.
A melody like that belongs in nothing less than his newly upgraded music box.
Not long afterward, Xiaoba invites you to admire his latest masterpiece!
This time, he has fitted the music box into a flaming arrow and then strapped the arrow to himself.
After "Skyward Soar," Xiaoba's newest invention, "Flying Singer," once again rings through the mountains.
May Xiaoba make another safe landing!

zh:
阿巧

别人家的狗会看门，阿巧会算数。
主人在案上做术数题，它就趴在一旁看。
“勾三，股四，弦几？”
主人敲敲桌案。
阿巧就汪汪汪汪汪，叫了五下。
“阿巧真聪明。”

阿巧陪着主人，从孤云的山，走到了滹沱河畔。
它算过，一共是，汪汪汪汪……叫不出多少汪的步。

它以为日子会一直这样算下去——
算雨，算星，算每天能跟着主人走多少步。

可某天晚上，主人却把它的绳子解开，在它头顶拍了一下，“阿巧，跟着星星跑吧，数到一万的时候，我就回来了。”

于是它跑啊跑啊，跑到气都喘不上来，
抬头一看——
满天都是星子。

它想，一万，要汪汪多少下呢。
en:
Clever

While other dogs guard doors, Clever does math.
When his master works on calculations at the desk, he lies nearby and watches.
"Base of three, altitude of four, what is the hypotenuse?"
The master taps the desk.
Clever goes woof, woof...barking five times.
"Clever boy."

Clever accompanied his master from the mountains of Lone Cloud to the banks of the Hutuo River.
He calculated it: a total of woof, woof, woof, woof... too many barks to count.

He thought days would go on being calculated like this...
Calculating the rain, the stars, and how many steps he could take with his master every day.

But one night, his master untied his leash and patted his head, "Clever, run with the stars. When you count to ten thousand, I'll be back."

So he ran and ran, until he was completely out of breath,
And looked up...
The sky was filled with stars.

He thought, how many barks would it take for ten thousand?

zh:
鹏也曾年轻过，年轻到能乘风而起九万里。
展翅千里的鲲鹏从十八层深渊一路奋力高飞，直飞到太阳上，把一缕缕金箔般的阳光叼下来塞进枯瘦的手中。

她和墨门里最常见的“天才”不同。
绝大多数“天才”无论如何惊才绝艳，总是只在书中、纸上和一件件器物里大展身手。
若让这群天才去和人打交道，去对贪婪的官爷们赔笑脸说好话却又分毫不让，塞半贯铜钱到狡诈的兵头手里换下一个瘸腿的半大孩子，或是让他们去对付把墨门借给他的粮种卖掉换酒的自暴自弃的村汉……
这群天才怕是只能笨拙地辩白几句，然后一个个哭着回山，回他们熟悉的纸堆里和器具间。

但鹏不一样。
鹏不只是高悬于空中的鸟，若有需要，她也可以成为沉在海中的鲲。
开源节流，争权夺利，八面玲珑、见风使舵、看人下菜……
只要能把粮食从有钱人嘴里抠出来塞进饥肠辘辘的另一张嘴里，她不介意与贪婪、愚蠢和荒谬为伍。

她最年轻的时候，做过一桩顶顶大的事——那还是长兴年间。
官府的农具质次价高，她见不得误了农时，便钻空子弄来一批拆卸方便的木板木轮，组成世人未曾见过的器具给几个村子用。
若上头的老爷们下来查，便是一堆不知何用的木板。
此事做得实在漂亮，就连收了她二钱碎银子的小吏巡视也忍不住啧舌。

鹏没错过这么一瞬的机会，沏了一壶农家的碎茶叶梗请他坐下。
那小吏望着麦田喝了她三大杯劣茶，临走时，忘了二钱银子在桌上。

她第二次见到这小吏是在县城的街上。
那小吏正啃着怀里冷硬的馒头，贴新税的告示。
见了她，便忍不住挺起胸膛，貌似不经意地提到他最近递的官呈，里头提了几笔诸如农时、官府农器、炉冶、巡检云云。
他不熟练地打着官腔，吹嘘自己说话颇有几分分量。
她笑着鼓掌。
“总有一天会的。”她说。

她是个无足轻重的人，他也是，还有很多或近或远的人们也是。
但是这些隔着千里万里，隔着官袍布衣，隔着书海麦浪的人如今走在同一条注定辉煌的大道上。
等那一天到来，所有为此努力过的同道都将欢呼着、大笑着，挥舞着他们的锄头、外衣或官帽，紧紧地互相拥抱在一起。
他们是渺小的，籍籍无名的。
他们是伟大的，永载青史的。

或许他的官呈真的被看见了，第三次见面来得并不慢。
很快，《许百姓自铸农器诏》和新收农器钱的告示便贴进了她常去的几个村子里。
他尚沾沾自喜于终于能让村里人用上便宜结实的自制农具，她却在阴凉处沉沉地盯着告示。
“……从前不收这个。”她说。
“从前都是买官府的，现在你们交点钱就能自己造，比之前划算多了。”
“你想，你租了人家的田，就得交租子。用了人家的路，就得交路费。这些钱都是有由头的，又没多收你。”
“……从前不收这个。”她又说。
“普天之下，莫非王土。就算之前不收，如今也该收了。”他气冲冲地走了。

来收村里的最后一具米肉的那天，他把自己吊死在了村口不远处的树上。只用了一条腰带。
她带了一壶茶坐在这片密密麻麻的坟岗前，倒了三大杯。

她喝下第一杯。
普天之下，莫非王土。
可那农具是我造出……它是我的，不是他们的。

她盛满第二杯。
农具不是，路也不是。
那路是村里几代人走出来的。它是先祖的，不是他们的。

她洒下第三杯。
村中的田地，也不是他们的。日月星辰，风土水火本无主，只是有人灵机一动指着一块地，高声叫嚷着这地是他的……

她在乌压压的坟前抬起手杖，像一杆长枪指着太阳。
那么，我宣布，此处是我的了。
en:
Peng had been young once, young enough to rise with the wind for ninety thousand li.

Like the great Peng of legend, she had fought her way up from the eighteen depths and flown all the way to the sun, only to snatch down strands of light like sheets of gold and press them into hands worn thin by hardship.
She was not like the sort of "genius" Mohist Hill produced so often.

Most geniuses, no matter how brilliant, shine only on the page, in their books, their papers, and the things they build. Put them in front of greedy officials and ask them to smile without giving an inch, to slip half a string of coins into the hand of a sly military underling to ransom a limping half-grown child, or to deal with some broken villager who sold off the Mohist Hill's seed grain for drink, and they would probably manage a few clumsy arguments before running back to the mountain in tears, back to the paper piles and workrooms they understood.
But Peng was different.

Peng was not only a bird high in the sky. When she had to be, she could also be the kun deep in the sea.
Cutting costs, finding new sources, fighting for leverage, reading the room, turning with the wind, dealing with people as they came... if it meant prying food out of one rich man's mouth and putting it into the mouth of someone starving, she did not mind keeping company with greed, stupidity, and absurdity.

When she was at her youngest, she pulled off something remarkable. This was back in the Changxing era.

The farm tools sold by the authorities were poor in quality and high in price. She could not bear to see the planting season wasted, so she found a loophole and got hold of a batch of wooden boards and wheels that could be taken apart easily, then assembled them into tools the world had never seen for several villages to use. If the men from above came down to inspect, all they would find was a pile of boards with no obvious purpose.
It was done so neatly that even the petty clerk who had taken her two mace of silver clicked his tongue in amazement during his inspection.

Peng did not miss the opening. She brewed a pot of rough village tea and invited him to sit.
The clerk sat looking out over the wheat fields and drank three large cups of bad tea. When he left, he forgot the silver on the table.

She saw him a second time on a county street. He was pasting up notices of a new tax while chewing on a cold, hard bun. When he spotted her, he could not help straightening up and casually bringing up a memorial he had submitted, one that mentioned things like the farming season, official farm tools, foundries, inspections, and the like.
He put on his official voice awkwardly enough, boasting that his words now carried some weight.
She smiled and clapped for him.

"One day they really will," she said.

She was insignificant. So was he. So were many others, near and far.
And yet all these people, separated by thousands upon thousands of li, by official robes and plain cloth, by seas of books and waves of wheat, were now walking the same road, one that was bound to shine.

When that day came, everyone who had worked for it would cheer and laugh, waving hoes, jackets, or official caps, and throw their arms around one another.
They were small, and nameless.
They were great, and they would be remembered.
Perhaps his memorial really was seen, because their third meeting came soon enough.

Before long, notices for the Edict Allowing Commoners to Forge Their Own Farm Tools, along with the new fee on such tools, were posted in the villages she often visited.
He was still pleased with himself, thinking he had finally helped the villagers get access to cheap, sturdy tools of their own. She, meanwhile, stood in the shade, staring at the notice for a long time.

"They never charged this before," she said.
"They used to make you buy from the authorities. Now you only pay a bit and make your own. That's a much better deal than before."
"If you rent someone's land, you pay rent. If you use someone's road, you pay a road fee. These things all have their reason. No one is charging you for nothing."
"They never charged this before," she said again.
"All land under heaven belongs to the ruler. Even if they did not charge it before, they should charge it now."

He stormed off.

On the day they came to collect the village's last grain and scraps of meat, he hanged himself from a tree not far from the village entrance, with nothing but a belt.
She brought a pot of tea and sat before that crowded field of graves, then poured three full cups.
She drank the first.

All land under heaven belongs to the ruler.
But I made those tools. They are mine, not theirs.

She filled the second.
The tools are not theirs. Neither is the road.
That road was worn into the ground by generations of villagers. It belongs to those who came before, not to them.

She poured out the third.
Nor do the fields belong to them. The sun and moon, the stars, the wind, the soil, the water, the fire, none of these had an owner to begin with. Someone simply had a clever thought one day, pointed at a piece of land, and shouted that it was his...

Before the dark press of graves, she raised her staff and pointed it at the sun like a spear.

"Then I declare this place mine."

zh:
田英疾驰在前往清风驿的路上，日夜兼程。
他跑死了三匹马，没有合过一次眼，只为了追上那场宴会。
那场他一手注定的清风驿之宴。

那一季的江南，雨多近妖，漫天的雨幕倾盆落下，将他所有行踪与气息尽悉隐匿。
这是一个刺客的天命之时。
就算浑身湿透、沾满泥泞，也依旧喜悦。因为他早已将自己置之度外。
他眼中只有一个目标，为了那个目标，他可以身死一万次，毫不足惜。
刀已经磨到最利，只等待翻开那人的血肉。

宴已开。
他终于等到了那个机会。
使者在门内醉醺醺地喘息，他在门外露出雪亮的匕首。
生与死，成与败，在这一瞬间，变得像这扇嘎吱作响的木门一样薄而脆弱。
推门，门开，使者惊慌的眼。
抬手，刀落，一切无声。
他走了，来无影，去无踪。

只在史书上留下这样一行字：
“唐人夜宴契丹使者于清风驿，酒酣，起更衣，久不返，视之，失其首矣。”
en:
Tian Ying races toward Breeze Post, riding through night and day without rest.
Three horses died beneath him, driven to exhaustion by his relentless pursuit. He never closes his eyes. All this is for a banquet.
A banquet at Qingfeng Post, one he himself has set into motion.

That spring in Jiangnan, the rain never ceases. It falls like a curtain drawn over the land, veiling all sound and sight, masking every step he leaves.
It is the destined time for the assassin.
Drenched and muddied, Tian Ying still feels joy. He has long since cast aside his own life.
Now, he lives for one purpose and will die a thousand times if it means fulfilling it.
His blade is honed to a whisper, longing to taste flesh and bone.

The banquet has begun.
At last, the moment arrives.
Inside, a drunken messenger wheezes and staggers. Outside, Tian Ying stands with a dagger in hand.
Life and death, victory and defeat, in that moment, are as brittle as the creaking wooden door.
He pushes it open. The messenger's eyes widen in panic.
The knife falls. Silence follows.
He vanishes as quietly as he comes.

Only one sentence is remembered in history:
"At Breeze Post, during a banquet hosted by the Later Tang Government to honor the Khitan envoy, the envoy, in a drunken stupor, left to change his clothes and was gone for a long time. When he was finally found, he had been decapitated."

zh:
榔头的脾气和榔头一样倔。但晦谷的大家伙都知道，榔头是最负责的狗。

在榔头的世界里，风是头号大敌，落叶是第二大敌。只要到了夜里，任何会动的东西都得被它汪汪两声。

直到它遇见了真正的宿敌——那只偷米的小贼。它铆足了劲儿，想用最洪亮的叫声吓跑对方，可换来的却不是嘉奖，而是主人的一顿训斥。

榔头委屈极了，它不明白，但它还是懂了一个新规矩：抓老鼠，不归它管。

吱吱吱——讨厌的老鼠又来了。
榔头动了动耳朵，把脑袋埋得更深了。

吱吱吱——汪！汪！汪！汪！
榔头站了起来，开始冲着米缸大叫。

虽然主人说了，狗拿耗子是多管闲事，但它就是要管！
en:
Hammer was as stubborn as his name. But everyone in Mirkvale knew: Hammer was the most responsible dog of all.

In Hammer's world, the wind was Enemy Number One. Falling leaves were Enemy Number Two. At night, anything that moved got a loud bark.

Until he met his true nemesis, the little thief who stole rice. He mustered all his strength, trying to scare it off with his mightiest bark. But instead of praise, he got scolded.

Hammer was heartbroken. He didn't understand. But he learned a new rule: catching mice was not his job.

Squeak squeak squeak. The annoying mouse again.
Hammer twitched his ears. Buried his head deeper.

Squeak squeak squeak. WOOF! WOOF! WOOF! WOOF!
Hammer stood up. He barked at the rice jar with all his might.

Master said dogs chasing mice was meddling. But he didn't care. He would meddle.

zh:
雨从午后开始下，直到傍晚时分也没停。
小鸭躺在洼地里，满身泥泞，翅膀上的血丝被雨水冲淡，渗进土里。
狐狸的气息早已散去，可这地方偏得很，来的人少，鸟兽也少，大约没谁会发现小鸭。
小鸭眯着眼，看天一点点黑下去……

忽然，有人路过。可小鸭的呼吸声太微弱，被雨盖住了大半。
那人没走多远，又退了回来，在小鸭身边停了片刻。
接着一只手探下来，袖口宽大，里子是干的。
小鸭被托起，身子轻飘飘的，像一片湿透的叶子。
它没挣扎……已经没力气了。

被塞进袖子的瞬间，暖意从四面八方裹过来，那是人的体温。
小鸭一点点醒过来，却闻到袖口沾着淡淡的血腥与锈气。
山下卖鸭羹的老汉，也有这个气味……
小鸭用尽最后一点气力，狠狠啄下去！
喙尖钝钝的，刺不破皮肉，只在那人手背上留下一个红印子。
他手臂微微一僵，却没收回去，只是把袖口拢得更紧了些。

剩下的路，小鸭是在颠簸中走完的。
什么也看不见，只有透过袖子传来的萤火微光。
那人提着一盏灯，灯影隔了层布，朦朦胧胧的，像隔着水看月亮。

小鸭再睁眼时，身下是干爽的蒲草，头顶是一片洞天。
它翻了翻身，发现翅膀被缠上布条，不松不紧，还打了个干净的结。
小鸭把脑袋埋进翅膀里，萤光不偏不倚，刚好笼住了蒲草铺成的小窝。
后来小鸭认得了这盏灯。也认得，灯光映亮的地方，就是家。

外边雨还在下，但淋不着它了。
en:
The rain had been falling since mid-afternoon, and even as dusk approached, it showed no signs of stopping.
A little duck lay stranded in a muddy hollow, completely coated in grime. Rainwater washed over its wing, diluting the streaks of blood and carrying them down into the soil.
The fox's scent had long since faded, but this was a desolate spot. With so few people or animals passing through, it was unlikely anyone would ever find the duck.
Through half-closed eyes, it watched the sky inch closer to pitch black...

Suddenly, someone walked by. But the duck's breathing was so shallow that the sound was almost entirely swallowed by the rain.
The passerby took a few more steps before hesitating, turning back, and pausing beside the tiny creature.
A hand reached down from a wide sleeve. The lining inside was dry.
As the duck was scooped up, it felt as weightless as a sodden leaf.
It didn't struggle. It simply had no strength left.

The moment it was tucked into the sleeve, warmth enveloped it from all sides. That was the comforting heat of a human body.
As the duck slowly roused, it caught a faint scent lingering on the cuff: a metallic tang of blood and rust.
It was the exact smell that clung to the old man who sold duck stew at the foot of the mountain.
Gathering every last ounce of its strength, the duck pecked hard at the person's hand!
But its blunt beak couldn't pierce the skin, leaving nothing but a small red welt on the back of the person's hand.
The arm stiffened for a second, but instead of pulling away, the person simply drew the sleeve more snugly around it.

The duck spent the rest of the journey jostling along in the dark.
It couldn't see a thing, save for a faint, firefly-like glow seeping through the fabric.
The person was carrying a lantern, its light softened and blurred by the cloth, like looking at the moon from underwater.

When the duck opened its eyes again, it was resting on a bed of crisp, dry reeds, safe beneath a sheltered roof.
It shifted its weight and noticed that its injured wing had been wrapped in a strip of cloth, not too tight, not too loose, and tied off with a neat knot.
The duck tucked its head back beneath its wing. The soft, firefly glow fell perfectly over its little reed nest.
In time, the little duck would come to recognize that lantern. It would learn that wherever its light fell, that place was home.

Outside, the rain was still falling, but it couldn't touch the duck anymore.

To him, being a wanderer meant drinking hard, eating well, cursing the heavens, and despising the corrupt. 
That is, until he met Wang Qing. 

It was Wang Qing who saved him when the Khitans rode through and plundered the fields. 
Armor battered, body bleeding, yet he removed that armor and gave it to Lie Yan. 
From that moment on, Lie Yan understood, there was another kind of hero in this world. 
Though dead, his chivalrous soul still shines bright among history's finest. 

From that day forward, Lie Yan vowed to become that kind of hero too.

As a child, she fled the blazing inferno that consumed the Zheng household, stumbling blindly into a pack of wolves. Raised by beasts, she forgot what it meant to be human, or even if she ever was one. 

Years later, in the dazzling lights of Ghost Revelry Hall, the Wolf Maiden who had long forgotten human speech saw something more vicious than any beast. The child fed by wolves came to remember the ugliness of humanity. 

Twice in her life, she ran from the world of men into the domain of wolves. The first time, she fled. The second, she returned home. 

To the world, she was a dog. To the wolves, she was one of their own.

zh:
十八岁那年，风雨飘摇的“又一楼”交到了余一美手里。
她天生一副识味辨火的七窍玲珑心，接手后，硬是凭着一手利落的刀工绝活，在酒肆林立的杭州城里杀出了威名。彼时双亲健在，为她相中了一门看似门当户对的姻亲。她将那男子请到店中，亲自下厨招待了一餐饭。待残席撤下、客出门后，她转头便对父母撂下一句：“这人，我不嫁。”

婚事虽黄，酒楼的生意却如烈火烹油。
余家大娘子做得一手细薄如雪的好鱼脍，寻常的春笋、秋莼等家常小鲜，经她之手亦能点化成舌尖绝味。哪怕是“钱王四喜鼎”这等讲究排场火候的王府大菜，她烹来也是游刃有余。

不仅如此，她还暗自将北方手艺融会贯通，变着法儿地推陈出新。
加上那条“只烹当日第一网鲜货，不鲜不收钱”的铁规矩，“又一楼”很快便成了满城权贵趋之若鹜的餐馆。
直到多年以后，那个曾被她拒之门外的男子在蕃坊赌场输得倾家荡产，众人才惊觉余掌柜当年那双毒辣的慧眼。有人好奇问起，她也只是慢条斯理地擦拭着杀鱼刀，淡然道：“吃相即本相。和人吃一餐饭，什么就都明白了。”
en:
Yu Yimei was eighteen when she took over Another Tavern. The place was barely staying afloat.
She had a born cook's feel for flavor and heat. Her deft knife work soon made her name in Hangzhou, a city teeming with taverns. Her parents were still alive then, and had found her a suitor whose family seemed a good match for their own. She invited him to the tavern and cooked him a meal herself. Once the table was cleared and he had left, she turned to her parents. "I'm not marrying him."

The match came to nothing. Business boomed.
Her raw fish came in slices thin as snowflakes. Even the simplest seasonal fare, spring bamboo shoots or autumn watershield, became something exquisite in her hands. She was just as deft with King Qian's Four-Delight Cauldron, a grand royal dish that called for lavish presentation and a sure hand at the stove.

She was quietly making northern techniques her own, too, constantly finding new ways to put them to use.
Her rule was absolute: "Only the day's first catch. If it isn't fresh, it's free." That promise soon helped make Another Tavern a favorite with the city's rich and powerful.
Years later, the man she'd turned down gambled away everything he owned at a gambling den in the foreign quarter. Only then did people realize how shrewd she'd been. Asked how she'd known, she slowly wiped down the knife she used for fish and said, "People show their true selves at the table. Share a meal with someone, and you'll know all you need to."

zh:
日头火热，张大爷时常拿着把蒲扇，蒲扇底下蹲着只猫，耳朵一抖一抖的，那就是扇儿。
没人说得清它什么时候开始跟着张大爷的。只晓得有一回暑气蒸人，张大爷坐在竹椅上摇扇子，一只猫从墙根底下钻出来，挨着椅子腿儿一趴，眼睛眯成一条缝，正正好好卡在扇风的范围里头。张大爷低头瞅了它一眼，扇子多摇了两下。
第二日，那猫又来了。
第三日，那猫把下巴搁在大爷的鞋面上，呼噜呼噜的，睡到了第四日，和往后的许多日。
帮它扇了这许多日，张大爷也没给它取个正经名儿。直到大爷的孙子说它专蹭扇子风，不如叫就叫“扇儿”。张大谷一听，哈哈笑起来。
“中！这名儿好，好记。”
张大爷日日帮它摇扇，都没能顾上自己，每每问起，大爷只说小猫崽毛多，比他更怕日头晒。
扇儿的确是怕热，大爷若是不摇扇，它就凑过去，用脑袋顶那扇子柄。张大爷笑骂：“你倒会支使人。”说着又摇起来，扇儿便重新趴下，眯着眼，尾巴一卷一卷的。
日头升起来，它就去大爷边上蹲着。日头落了，它跟着张大爷在院子里转。月亮出来了，它缩在大爷脚边，呼噜声和着虫鸣。
后来松风居的学子们都认得扇儿，谁要是拿着蒲扇路过，它便抬头看一眼，不是它认识的那把扇子，它便不动，是了，它只认张大爷手里那一把。
旁人的扇子，扇不出那个风。
en:
On scorching days, Grandpa Zhang could often be found with a palm-leaf fan in hand, and beneath that fan, a cat with ears twitching this way and that. That was Shan'er.
No one could say quite when it had taken to following Grandpa Zhang about. It was only known that one sweltering day, when the heat pressed down like a smothering cloth, Grandpa Zhang sat in his bamboo chair fanning himself, and a cat crept out from beneath the base of the wall. It settled itself against the chair leg, eyes narrowed, and positioned itself precisely within the reach of the fan's breeze. Grandpa Zhang glanced down at it, and gave the fan a few extra strokes.
On the second day, the cat came again.
On the third day, the cat rested its chin upon the top of the old man's shoe and purred, and slept through to the fourth day, and through many days that followed.
For all those days of fanning, Grandpa Zhang had never thought to give it a proper name. It was his grandson who finally said that since it did nothing but seek out the fan's breeze, it may as well be called "Shan'er," meaning Little Fan. Grandpa Zhang heard this and burst out laughing.
"Aye, that'll do! A fine name. Easy to remember."
Day after day, Grandpa Zhang fanned it, often forgetting to fan himself at all. Whenever anyone remarked upon it, the old man only said that the little cat had far more fur than he did and suffered the sun far worse.
Shan'er did indeed loathe the heat. If the old man stopped fanning, it would nudge its way over and butt its head against the fan's handle. Grandpa Zhang would laugh and scold it: "You certainly know how to put a man to work." And then he would fan again, and Shan'er would settle back down, eyes half-shut, tail curling and uncurling.
When the sun rose, it went and crouched at the old man's side. When the sun set, it followed Grandpa Zhang on his rounds of the courtyard. When the moon came out, it curled at his feet, its purring mingling with the song of the insects.
In time, all the students of Pine Breeze Lodge came to know Shan'er. If anyone passed by carrying a palm-leaf fan, it would lift its head and look, but if it was not the fan it knew, it would not stir. Indeed, it had eyes for only the one in Grandpa Zhang's hand.
Another person's fan simply could not stir the same breeze.

zh: 文津馆以十相为尊，十相以双元为首，文元先于武元。除双元外，余八相无分高下先后。馆中大小诸务，十相皆列席共议。若有纷争，则召十相合决之。若十相之位有缺，则当集现任诸相，于馆中择贤补之。至于文元、武元之更替，必合三事：其一，前任文元所推；其二，十相俱无异议；其三，其人于文津馆立显赫之功。文津馆人才济济，然堪任十相者殊寡。赖此制遴选，宁缺毋滥，终得英才，众咸心服。
en: The Inkbound Order holds the Ten Sages in highest honor, with the Twin Mavens standing foremost among them, and the Laureate taking precedence over the Champion. Save for the Twin Mavens, the remaining eight Sages are ranked neither above nor below one another. All matters great and small within the Order are brought before the Ten Sages in joint deliberation. Should any dispute arise, the Ten Sages are convened to reach a collective resolution. Should a seat among the Ten Sages fall vacant, the sitting Sages are gathered to select a worthy soul from within the Order to fill it. As for the succession of the Laureate and the Champion, three conditions must be met: first, nomination by the preceding Laureate; second, unanimous approval from the Ten Sages; third, the candidate must have rendered distinguished service to the Inkbound Order. The Inkbound Order is not lacking in talent, yet those truly fit to serve among the Ten Sages are exceedingly few. By this system of selection, the Order holds to the principle of leaving a seat empty rather than filling it poorly, and in the end, only the truly worthy are chosen, to the wholehearted accord of all.

zh: 相传梨园的万春姑娘“一笑可抵万千春”，若是有缘之人更可得佳人“相携照影”之礼。有游侠倾慕许久，特车马百里亲至太湖，为求一睹芳颜。然万春姑娘终藏身帘后，避而不见。后一壮汉从帘后迎出，绝口不提万春之名，只邀来客纵情游览山水。来客只觉是万春姑娘羞于礼法，遂客从主便，伺机打探佳人轶事。然太湖山水旖旎，游侠亦沉醉其中，兴之所至，便与那壮汉借酒意酣然共舞，畅快非常。辞别之日，游侠虽抱憾未能一睹佳人倩影，却也幸与壮汉意气相投。殊不知那游览山川，酣然共舞之乐，正是江湖艳羡的“相携照影”……
en: Legend speaks of a beauty whose smile could outshine spring. Only the truly destined may perform the "Paired Radiance" with her. A wanderer sought her, but she stayed hidden; instead, a burly man invited him to revel and dance. Though the wanderer never saw the beauty, their bond endured. Unbeknownst to him, their shared joy was the true Paired Radiance envied by all.
[Weekly] Import one Path Code ({0}/1)

十方信众，共襄善举；功德一瓦，录此芳名。
佛光宝聚，如积善行；梵呗轻弥，似留余声。
故为此簿，惟愿诸君：常怀照灼之心，永念慈悲之音。

Devotees from all directions, brought together by fate; gathering and parting, bound by Buddhist karma.
Followers from the ten directions, united in good deeds; each merit recorded, their names enshrined here.
Like accumulating virtuous deeds, the light of Buddha gathers; like lingering chants, the echoes of compassion remain.
Thus, this register is made, wishing all: may your hearts ever shine with wisdom, and your minds forever resonate with mercy.

江湖上的面吃个新鲜，家里的面才是念想。胃里装点家乡的热乎气，走到哪儿脚下都稳当。
新的一岁，可要照顾好自己。今年不好祝你长个头了，就祝你像你小时候说的那样，成为一个大侠！
要是累了，就回来歇歇。酒厂里又有了新酒，就等你来开坛了。到时候给咱们讲讲外头的事儿，不醉不归！
en:
Happy Birthday, Young Master!
Everyone back in the village misses you. We knew your birthday was coming up, so we all pitched in to make you a bowl of longevity noodles and had them sent your way. Make sure to eat them while they're hot! And remember, slurp the whole noodle down in one go without biting it. It's good luck for a long, smooth life!
The food out in the jianghu might be a nice change of pace, but nothing hits the spot quite like a taste of home. With a warm hometown meal in your belly, you'll walk a little steadier wherever your travels take you.
You're another year older now, so make sure you're taking good care of yourself. I suppose it's too late to wish for a growth spurt, so instead, I'll just wish for you to become a celebrated wanderer as you dreamed in your childhood!
Whenever you get tired, come home and rest your feet for a while. We've got a fresh batch of wine brewing at the winery, just waiting for you to crack the seal. You can tell us all your stories from the outside world, and we'll drink the night away!

同行的教坊乐师剥开了雪白的果肉，而三娘只想将它留下。

之后天子和贵妃喜爱她唱江南吉州小调，又赞“喉转一声，响传九陌”。
在御前畏畏缩缩的小娃儿，成了闻名长安的永新娘子。
她唱“北斗酌美酒，劝龙各一觞”，唱高台郎月，喜者闻之气勇，愁者闻之肠绝。
春日得赐的那枚荔枝，被她收在枕边，直到腐坏枯萎。
王朝的腐坏，并不比荔枝来得晚。
洎渔阳之乱，六宫星散。她流落广陵，江上唱“平沙落日大荒西，陇上明星高复低”，却听得有人泣泪相和。
金吾将军也好，绝世名伶也罢，今夜不过飘摇孤舟。

离人忆长安，言谈中她恍然想起梨花散坠的那个春日。
那位女子已成了马嵬坡一缕芳魂。
三娘再也无缘问她，这首曲子，你是否真心喜爱？
en:
The choicest fruit grows only in the dreams of those who gather it. 
Rushed from Lingnan by swift horses, this rare delicacy was so precious that even a mere glance was a privilege denied to ordinary folk. 
While the troupe's musicians eagerly peeled back its snow-white flesh, Sanniang only wished she could keep it a secret, a treasure all her own. 

Later, the Emperor and the Noble Consort delighted in her singing—a tender folk tune from the southern lands. They praised her voice, saying, "Her clear voice sends echoes weaving through every street and alleyway." 
That timid child who once trembled before the imperial throne blossomed into Lady Eternal Renewal, a name on the lips of all Chang'an. 
Her song echoes beneath the bright moon atop the lofty pavilion, stirring courage in the joyful and wrenching sorrow in the broken-hearted. 
That lychee, gifted on a spring day, lay beside her pillow—cherished until it withered and decayed. 
The rot of the dynasty came no slower than that of the fruit. 
When the rebellion shattered the palace and scattered the sovereignty, she found herself adrift in distant lands. Her sorrowful melodies were met by tearful echoes in kind. 
Whether mighty generals or performers unmatched in skill, that night all were but solitary boats adrift on a stormy sea. 

The exiled soul carried memories of Chang'an close, and in quiet moments recalled a spring day, when pear blossoms fell like drifting snow. 
The woman from that day had become nothing more than a lingering fragrance on a barren slope. 
Sanniang would never again have the chance to ask her: "Did you truly love this song?"

zh:
不孝儿君皓书：
儿君皓顿首，数年不见，愧对阿母。今冬甚寒，阿母尚安耶？
若阿母问父事，儿诚言，昔年阿父以偷盗闻名，儿深感不耻。
故离家西行，远拜天泉，今又入燕北盟，捍卫家国。
十年倏忽而过，今每思之闻之，方知昔年阿父所为，皆是侠盗之义。
怨怼多年，错怪多年，若阿母见信，望阿母替儿为父赔罪，儿泣言。
然恕儿不能回乡，尽孝二老膝前。
今山河破碎，北蛮长驱，儿当以己身，为百姓关，为山河关。
若清河破，则千万之家，陷乱离也。
恕儿一意孤行，今付家书，托丰禾村友人传之，望阿母，阿父，勿挂勿念！
en:
Your unfilial son Junhao writes:
I bow my head in shame, for years have passed since we last met, and I feel deep guilt before you, Mother. This winter is bitterly cold—are you well?
Should you ask about Father, I must confess: in my youth, I was mortified by his reputation as a thief.
That is why I left home to travel west, seeking enlightenment at the Well of Heaven, and now I have joined the Northern Vow to defend our homeland.
Ten years have flown by, and only now—through reflection and hearsay—do I realize Father's deeds were those of a chivalrous thief, not mere thievery.
I harbored resentment and misunderstood him for so long. If you receive this letter, Mother, please convey my apologies to him on my behalf. I write this in tears.
Forgive me for being unable to return home and serve you both at your knees.
Our land lies broken, and northern barbarians advance unhindered. I must be a barrier for the people, a bulwark for our rivers and mountains.
If Qinghe falls, countless families will be thrown into chaos.
Forgive my single-minded resolve. I entrust this letter to a friend from Harvestfall Village. Please, Mother and Father—do not worry or miss me!

鯚鱼即鳜鱼，在南宋的《梦粱录》和《武林旧事》中，鳜鱼都称鯚鱼，据汪曾祺考证，此名来源于罽花。罽花是一种彩色的毛织品，上面的花纹同鳜鱼相似，后人因嫌“罽”字复杂，便写成了“鯚”。此鱼食性凶猛，只吃活鱼活虾，因此肉质细腻，是最美味的淡水鱼之一。
en:
Cherry petals fleck the traveler's cloak as plump mandarin fish in streams soak. 

Chinese Perch, known today as the Mandarin Fish, it was recorded in Southern Song texts like Dreams of Splendor and Old Tales of the Martial World. Its name derives from the Ji flower, a type of brocade whose intricate patterns mirror the fish's scales. Because the character of Ji was hard to write, people instead used a character of the same pronunciation to represent the fish. Because it feeds only on live prey.Its flesh is particularly tender, making it one of the most prized freshwater delicacies.

zh:
据父母说，她刚学会走路时，便喜欢到处跑。
明明小短腿还算不得结实，一不小心便磕了、碰了、摔了，可一爬起来，拍拍屁股，还是要跑。
或者并不是跑，而是追？
她似乎总有些要追的东西。蝴蝶、风絮、飞花、萤火……她喜欢去追，去看——这一切充满生机，她不曾知晓的新奇之物。
可这么磕碰下去，小娃自己不在意，却摔疼了父母的心。于是手巧的父亲做了支小鱼竿，又寻来颗晶莹剔透的琉璃石头作钓饵，自然不为钓鱼，而是钓住自家小娃。

阳光下，那颗闪闪发光的琉璃石头被高高挂起，她追着玩了许久许久。直到夜幕低垂，琉璃石头的光暗了下去。可这一次，她却没有低下头去寻些别的物件来追，她仍抬着头望向高处。这一次，她眼眸中闪耀着的，是那片万古未变的星海。
这星海，真的不曾变过吗？不，这些星星，原来是活的。
这繁复的星图，交错的星轨；这一颗又一颗不遵从预测，自顾自乱走的星子；这或许穷尽一生也无法完全了解的星空。
原来天上竟藏着一方生机盎然的新世界，藏着或许穷尽一生，也无法全部知晓的无尽奥秘……
人都会长大，长大了，知道得多了，便习以为常。

那是蝴蝶，那是风絮，那是飞花，那是萤火——那是星星。
长大了，知道会摔倒，便不喜再去追。
可她已着了迷，坠入这星海之中。
她磕着、碰着、摔着、追着，一如孩童时候。
en:
Her parents used to say that as soon as she learned to walk, she wanted to run everywhere. Her little legs were still unsteady, so she was always tripping, stumbling, and falling. But every time she got back up, dusted herself off, and ran right on.
Or perhaps it was not running at all, but chasing.

She always seemed to have something to chase. Butterflies, drifting catkins, falling petals, fireflies... She loved to run after them, to watch them, to marvel at all the lively, unfamiliar things she had never known before.
She never minded the bumps and bruises herself, but each fall made her parents' hearts ache. So her clever-handed father made her a little fishing rod and found a clear, gleaming piece of colored glass for bait. It was not meant to catch fish, of course, but his own little girl.

In the sunlight, that shining glass stone was hung high above her, and she chased it for the longest time. At last night fell, and its glow began to fade. But this time, she did not lower her head to look for something else to chase. She kept looking up.
And this time, what shone in her eyes was that ancient sea of stars.

Had it truly never changed? No. The stars were alive.
There were intricate star charts, crossing celestial paths, and star after star that paid no heed to prediction and wandered where they pleased. There was a sky so vast that one could spend a lifetime studying it and still never know it all.
So above her was a living new world, full of vitality and endless mysteries, more than any one life could ever uncover...

People grow up. And when they do, when they learn more and more, they begin to take such things for granted.
That is a butterfly. That is drifting catkins. That is a falling petal. That is a firefly. That is a star.

Once people know they might fall, they no longer like to chase.
But she had already fallen for that sea of stars.

She kept stumbling, bumping, falling, and chasing, just as she had when she was a child.

鹏长老尊鉴
前蒙长老冒死争时，桑得以脱身，然弟子愚顽，潜行折返，空负深恩，唯请长老恕。
今桑所以甘蹈死地者，非不信杜重威卖墨门之事，实因莜麦将熟，终须竟其末录。自唐末岁以来，寒日愈酷，百稼凋萎。弟子遍访北地，偶得莜麦一种，耐霜雪而葆生机。幸得县令陈公信重，于栾城郊野试种三载，乃略通其性。今岁若得盈收，则非独栾城，举郡寒庶，皆可赖此全活。
幸得天佑，莜麦之植术已悉录无遗，吾心乃安。
契丹铁骑已近，弟子途穷，必无幸理。然长老武略超群，宵小当不足为害。倘见此笺，伏乞将弟子所录莜麦耕植要术，付与栾城柴伯约。若得如此，则桑虽葬身荒野，亦不枉矣。
弟子柴桑顿首拜别。
en:
To Elder Peng, with deepest respect,
It was only because you risked your life to buy me a little time that I managed to get away. Yet I, foolish and headstrong, turned back in secret and so proved unworthy of such great kindness. I ask only that you forgive me.
The reason I now go willingly into mortal danger is not because I doubt that Du Chongwei has sold out Mohist Hill. It is because the oats are nearly ripe, and I must see this final record through to the end. Since the closing years of the Tang, the cold has grown harsher year by year, and the crops have steadily failed. I traveled throughout the northern lands and by chance came upon a kind of oat that can endure frost and snow without losing its vigor. Thanks to Magistrate Chen's trust, I was allowed to test its cultivation for three years in the fields outside Luancheng, and only then did I begin to understand its nature. If this year yields a full harvest, then it is not only Luancheng that may benefit. All the poor who struggle through the cold across the commandery may survive because of it.
By Heaven's grace, the methods for planting and cultivating oats have now been fully recorded without omission, and my heart is finally at peace.
The Khitan cavalry is already close at hand. I have reached the end of the road, and there can be no hope of escape. But your martial skill is beyond compare, and such petty villains should not be enough to threaten you. If this letter reaches you, I beg that the essential methods I have recorded for the Oat Cultivation Techniques be delivered to Chai Boyue of Luancheng. If that can be done, then even if I am buried in the wilderness, my death will not have been in vain.
Your disciple, Chai Sang, bows and takes his leave.

zh:
生蓬户之侧陋兮，不闲习于文符。不见图画之妙像兮，不闻先哲之典谟。既愚陋而寡识兮，谬忝厕于紫庐。非草苗之所处兮，恒怵惕以忧惧。怀思慕之忉怛兮，兼始终之万虑。嗟隐忧之忱积兮，独郁结而靡诉。意惨愦而无聊兮，思缠绵以增慕。夜耿耿而不寐兮，魂憧憧而至曙。风骚骚而四起兮，霜皑皑而依庭。日晻暧而无光兮，气懰栗以冽清。怀愁戚之多感兮，患涕泪之自零。

昔伯瑜之婉娈兮，每彩衣以娱亲。悼今日之乖隔兮，奄与家为参辰。岂相去之云远兮，曾不盈乎数寻。何宫禁之清切兮，欲瞻睹而莫因。仰行云以歔欷兮，涕流射而沾巾。惟屈原之哀感兮，嗟悲伤于离别。彼城阙之作诗兮，亦以日而喻月。况骨肉之相于兮，永缅邈而两绝。长含哀而抱戚兮，仰苍天而泣血。

乱曰：骨肉至亲，化为他人，永长辞兮。惨怆愁悲，梦想魂归，见所思兮。惊寤号啕，心不自聊，泣涟洏兮。援笔舒情，涕泪增零，诉斯诗兮。
en:
Born behind a humble gate of reeds, obscure and poor,
I never learned the written word in full.
No wondrous form of painting met my eye,
Nor ever reached my ears the wisdom of the sages old.
Dull and unknowing, of little wit,
By error I was brought into the palace halls.
This was no place for common grass to grow,
And so I lived in fear from day to day.
I bear the pain of longing in my heart,
And ten thousand cares for all that is to come.
Alas, these hidden sorrows deepen ever more,
Shut in alone, with no one there to hear.
My thoughts are troubled, desolate, and spent,
And longing winds more tightly still about my chest.
Through the long night I lie and cannot sleep,
My soul unquiet till the edge of dawn.
The wind stirs low on every side,
White frost lies thick along the court.
The sun is dim and gives no warmth,
The air is bitter, clear, and cold.
So laden am I with grief and sorrow
That tears must fall of themselves.

Think of Bo Yu, gentle and dutiful,
Who wore bright robes to delight his parents.
But I lament the cruel sundering of this day,
For now my kin and I are parted like Shen and Chen.
How can the distance between us be called far?
It is not even the span of a few paces.
Yet so cold and strict are the palace walls
That though I long to see them, I find no way.
I lift my eyes to the drifting clouds
And my tears fall, wetting my kerchief through.
Think of Qu Yuan and the grief he bore,
The sorrow of parting that he sang.
And those who wrote of towers and city walls,
Using sun and moon to speak of separation.
How much more bitter for those of one blood,
Now cast apart and cut off from each other.
Long have I carried grief and made my dwelling with sorrow,
Looking to Heaven and weeping tears of blood.

Envoy
Those bound to me by blood, my dearest kin,
Have become as strangers, lost to me afar.
In sorrow and anguish my soul returns in dreams,
And there I see the ones I long for.
But waking in alarm, I cry aloud,
My heart unable to endure the pain,
My tears falling without end.
So I take up the brush and set down all that stirs within me,
And with tears still falling, entrust it to this poem.

zh:
酒蒙子最开始没有名字，它在山间野地里扑麻雀，在泥地里打滚儿，饱一顿饿一顿地流浪。
直到它遇见了一个一袭红衣的女人，时不时在路边给它放些肉骨头、剩了一半的鱼肉饭。
那女人总是风风火火地来，步履匆匆地去，身上梨花掺着酒味，一路嗅着这味道准能找到她放的吃食。
可是后来，女人很久没来，酒蒙子又开始流浪，但这次不一样了，它格外喜欢闻酒味，酒的味道就是家的味道。它边走边玩，玩得筋疲力尽了就随便找个酒缸趴着喝酒，还没舔几口呢，就醉得不行，竟迷迷糊糊地跳上了运酒的车，醉醺醺的从清河到了开封。
因为车上都是酒，它下车时还浑身带着酒气嘞！这可真是稀奇事儿，村民们一传十十传百，都说村子里的运酒车上跳下来只怪狗，是个酒蒙子。酒蒙子快活地摇着尾巴，痴迷地闻着这熟悉的酒香，仿佛回到了有那女人的时光。酒蒙子喜欢这里，这里到处都是酒味，到处都是家。
en:
Boozer starts with no name, pouncing on sparrows in the wild hills, rolling in mud, surviving meal to meal as a stray.
Then he meets a woman in red who sometimes leaves him meaty bones, half-finished fish meals by the roadside.
She always comes in a hurry, leaves in a hurry, smelling of pear blossoms and wine. Following that scent, he always finds her offerings.
But one day, she stops coming. Boozer wanders again, but something has changed. He loves the smell of wine now. Wine smells like home. He travels and plays, and when tired, he flops by any wine jar he finds, lapping at it until he gets dizzy, until one day he stumbles onto a wine cart and wakes up in Kaifeng, reeking of alcohol.
The villagers whisper: a strange dog, a drunkard, has jumped off their wine cart.
Boozer wags his tail, drunk on the familiar scent, feeling close to that woman again. He loves it here. Everywhere smells like wine. Everywhere smells like home.

zh:
【祭义第二十四】

祭不欲数，数则烦，烦则不敬。祭不欲疏，疏则怠，怠则忘。是故君子合诸天道：春禘秋尝。霜露既降，君子履之，必有凄怆之心，非其寒之谓也。春，雨露既濡，君子履之，必有怵惕之心，如将见之。乐以迎来，哀以送往，故禘有乐而尝无乐。致齐于内，散齐于外。齐之日：思其居处，思其笑语，思其志意，思其所乐，思其所嗜。齐三日，乃见其所为齐者。祭之日：入室，僾然必有见乎其位，周还出户，肃然必有闻乎其容声，出户而听，忾然必有闻乎其叹息之声。是故，先王之孝也，色不忘乎目，声不绝乎耳，心志嗜欲不忘乎心。致爱则存，致悫则着。着存不忘乎心，夫安得不敬乎？君子生则敬养，死则敬享，思终身弗辱也。君子有终身之丧，忌日之谓也。忌日不用，非不祥也。言夫日，志有所至，而不敢尽其私也。唯圣人为能飨帝，孝子为能飨亲。飨者，乡也。乡之，然后能飨焉。是故孝子临尸而不怍。君牵牲，夫人奠盎。君献尸，夫人荐豆。卿大夫相君，命妇相夫人。齐齐乎其敬也，愉愉乎其忠也，勿勿诸其欲其飨之也。文王之祭也：事死者如事生，思死者如不欲生，忌日必哀，称讳如见亲。祀之忠也，如见亲之所爱，如欲色然；其文王与？《诗》云：“明发不寐，有怀二人。”文王之诗也。祭之明日，明发不寐，飨而致之，又从而思之。祭之日，乐与哀半；飨之必乐，已至必哀。
仲尼尝，奉荐而进其亲也悫，其行趋趋以数。已祭，子赣问曰：“子之言祭，济济漆漆然；今子之祭，无济济漆漆，何也？”子曰：“济济者，容也远也；漆漆者，容也自反也。容以远，若容以自反也，夫何神明之及交，夫何济济漆漆之有乎？反馈，乐成，荐其荐俎，序其礼乐，备其百官。君子致其济济漆漆，夫何慌惚之有乎？夫言，岂一端而已？夫各有所当也。”
孝子将祭，虑事不可以不豫；比时具物，不可以不备；虚中以治之。宫室既修，墙屋既设，百物既备，夫妇齐戒沐浴，盛服奉承而进之，洞洞乎，属属乎，如弗胜，如将失之，其孝敬之心至也与！荐其荐俎，序其礼乐，备其百官，奉承而进之。于是谕其志意，以其恍惚以与神明交，庶或飨之。“庶或飨之”，孝子之志也。孝子之祭也，尽其悫而悫焉，尽其信而信焉，尽其敬而敬焉，尽其礼而不过失焉。进退必敬，如亲听命，则或使之也。孝子之祭，可知也，其立之也敬以诎，其进之也敬以愉，其荐之也敬以欲；退而立，如将受命；已彻而退，敬齐之色不绝于面。孝子之祭也，立而不诎，固也；进而不愉，疏也；荐而不欲，不爱也；退立而不如受命，敖也；已彻而退，无敬齐之色，而忘本也。如是而祭，失之矣。孝子之有深爱者，必有和气；有和气者，必有愉色；有愉色者，必有婉容。孝子如执玉，如奉盈，洞洞属属然，如弗胜，如将失之。严威俨恪，非所以事亲也，成人之道也。
先王之所以治天下者五：贵有德，贵贵，贵老，敬长，慈幼。此五者，先王之所以定天下也。贵有德，何为也？为其近于道也。贵贵，为其近于君也。贵老，为其近于亲也。敬长，为其近于兄也。慈幼，为其近于子也。是故至孝近乎王，至弟近乎霸。至孝近乎王，虽天子，必有父；至弟近乎霸，虽诸侯，必有兄。先王之教，因而弗改，所以领天下国家也。子曰：“立爱自亲始，教民睦也。立教自长始，教民顺也。教以慈睦，而民贵有亲；教以敬长，而民贵用命。孝以事亲，顺以听命，错诸天下，无所不行。”

en:
【Sacrificial Righteousness, Chapter 24】

Sacrifice should not be too frequent, for frequency leads to weariness, and weariness leads to irreverence. Sacrifice should not be too infrequent, for infrequency leads to neglect, and neglect leads to forgetfulness. Therefore, the noble person aligns with the ways of Heaven: spring di sacrifice and autumn chang sacrifice. When frost and dew descend, the noble person steps upon them and inevitably feels a sorrowful heart—not because of the cold itself. In spring, when rain and dew moisten the earth, the noble person steps upon them and inevitably feels a startled, reverent heart, as if about to see the departed. Joy is used to welcome their coming; grief is used to see them off. Thus, the di sacrifice has music, while the chang sacrifice has none. One maintains inner purification and outer discipline. On the days of purification: one thinks of their dwelling place, thinks of their laughter and speech, thinks of their aspirations and intentions, thinks of what brought them joy, thinks of what they cherished. After three days of purification, one can truly see the one for whom the purification is undertaken. On the day of sacrifice: entering the chamber, one seems to see them in their place; turning about and exiting the door, one seems to hear their voice and bearing; leaving the door and listening, one seems to hear their sighs. Thus, in the filial piety of the former kings, their countenance was never forgotten by the eyes, their voice never ceased in the ears, their aspirations and desires were never forgotten in the heart. When love is utmost, they remain present; when sincerity is utmost, they become manifest. When manifest and present, never forgotten in the heart—how could one not be reverent? The noble person, while they live, serves them with reverence; when they die, honors them with sacrifice, thinking throughout life never to disgrace them. The noble person has a lifelong mourning—this refers to the death anniversary. On the death anniversary, one does not engage in other affairs—not because it is inauspicious, but because on that day, one's thoughts are fully directed elsewhere, and one dares not indulge in personal matters. Only the sage can offer sacrifice to the Emperor of Heaven; only the filial son can offer sacrifice to his parents. To offer sacrifice means to face toward them. Facing toward them, then one can truly offer sacrifice. Therefore, the filial son stands before the personator without shame. The lord leads the sacrificial victim; the lady pours the libation from the ewer. The lord presents offerings to the personator; the lady presents the dishes of grain. The ministers and great officers assist the lord; the honored ladies assist the lady. How solemn is their reverence, how harmonious their loyalty, how earnest their desire that the sacrifice be accepted! When King Wen offered sacrifice: he served the dead as he served the living, thought of the departed so much that he wished not to live, was always grieved on the death anniversary, and spoke of the tabooed name as if seeing the parent. Such sincerity in sacrifice, seeing what the parent loved, as if yearning for it—was this not King Wen? The Book of Songs says: "Sleepless until dawn, thinking of those two." This is a poem about King Wen. The day after the sacrifice, sleepless until dawn, having offered and brought them near, he continued to think of them. On the day of sacrifice, joy and grief were equal: in the offering there must be joy; when they have come and gone, there must be grief.
Confucius once performed the chang sacrifice, presenting the offerings to his parents with utmost sincerity, walking quickly and hurriedly. After the sacrifice, Zigong asked: "You have said that in sacrifice one should be solemn and composed, dignified and self-reflective. Yet in your own sacrifice today, there was none of this solemnity or composure. Why?" The Master said: "Solemnity is an appearance of distance; composure is an appearance of self-reflection. If one's appearance is distant, or if one's appearance is self-reflective, how can one commune with the spirits? What place is there for solemnity and composure? When the offerings are returned, the music is complete, the offerings and stands are presented, the rites and music are ordered, and all the officers are in readiness—then the noble person may display his solemnity and composure. But what room is there for such bearing when one is in the presence of the departed? My words—do they apply to only one situation? Each has its proper application."
When the filial son is about to sacrifice, he must prepare his thoughts in advance; when the time comes, he must have all things ready; he empties his mind to manage the affair. The palace chambers being repaired, the walls and rooms being set in order, all things being prepared, the husband and wife fast and bathe, don their finest garments, and present the offerings with reverence—so earnest, so attentive, as if they could not bear the weight, as if about to lose it—is this not the utmost of filial reverence and devotion! They present the offerings and stands, order the rites and music, prepare all the officers, and present everything with reverence. Then they communicate their intentions, and in that dim and indistinct state commune with the spirits, hoping perhaps that they will partake. "Hoping perhaps they will partake"—this is the filial son's aspiration. In the filial son's sacrifice, he exhausts his sincerity and is sincere, exhausts his faith and is faithful, exhausts his reverence and is reverent, exhausts the rites without error. In advancing and retreating, he must be reverent, as if hearing his parents' commands, as if being directed by them. The filial son's sacrifice can be known: when he stands, he is reverent and humble; when he advances, he is reverent and joyful; when he presents offerings, he is reverent and desirous; when he withdraws and stands, it is as if about to receive a command; when the offerings are removed and he withdraws, a reverent and solemn expression never leaves his face. In the filial son's sacrifice, if he stands without humility, he is stubborn; if he advances without joy, he is distant; if he presents offerings without desire, he lacks love; if he withdraws and stands without receiving a command, he is arrogant; if after the offerings are removed he withdraws without a reverent and solemn expression, he has forgotten his roots. To sacrifice in such a manner is to fail in it. The filial son who has deep love must have a harmonious spirit; one with a harmonious spirit must have a joyful countenance; one with a joyful countenance must have a gentle bearing. The filial son is like one holding jade, like one holding a brimming vessel—earnest and attentive, as if unable to bear the weight, as if about to lose it. Stern威严 and solemn dignity are not the way to serve one's parents; they belong to the way of adulthood.
There are five things by which the former kings governed the world: honoring the virtuous, honoring the noble, honoring the aged, respecting the elder, and cherishing the young. These five are how the former kings established order in the world. Why honor the virtuous? Because they are close to the Dao. Why honor the noble? Because they are close to the ruler. Why honor the aged? Because they are close to one's parents. Why respect the elder? Because they are close to one's elder brothers. Why cherish the young? Because they are close to one's children. Therefore, utmost filial piety approaches kingly virtue, and utmost brotherly respect approaches hegemonic power. Utmost filial piety approaches kingly virtue—even the Son of Heaven must have a father; utmost brotherly respect approaches hegemonic power—even the feudal lords must have elder brothers. The teachings of the former kings, followed without alteration, are how they led the world and the states. The Master said: "Establish love beginning with one's parents, to teach the people harmony. Establish teaching beginning with one's elders, to teach the people obedience. Teach kindness and harmony, and the people will value their kin; teach respect for elders, and the people will value following commands. With filial piety to serve one's parents and obedience to follow commands, apply this throughout the world, and nothing will fail to be accomplished."

zh:
一画师偶得古卷残页，绘山川城池，人物栩栩如生。他醉心临摹，渐觉身边景物周遭浮现墨痕，人声如念戏文。
一夜，油灯摇曳，他窥见画纸边缘竟有未干的墨渍延伸而出，连接着自家墙壁！惊骇中，他提笔蘸墨，颤抖着在“自家”屋角添了一笔。霎时天旋地转，墙壁如宣纸般皱缩剥落，露出其后的宣纸与画轴木杆。
他方才明悟，自己连同这方天地，不过是某幅巨画上几滴将干的墨痕。画外似有低语传来：“这一笔……倒是多余了。” 话音落，画师与他的小屋，如被清墨抚去，只余古卷上一处新添的、微不足道的墨点。
en:
A painter came across the torn remnants of an ancient scroll, its mountains, cities, and figures rendered so finely they seemed almost alive. He lost himself in copying it, and after some time he began to notice faint traces of ink appearing in the world around him, with voices that murmured like players reciting from a script.
One night, by the unsteady light of his oil lamp, he noticed that the wet ink at the edge of the scroll had spread beyond the paper and was seeping into the walls of his room. Seized with dread, he took up his brush, dipped it, and with a trembling hand added a single stroke to a corner of what he now thought of as his room. The world lurched. The walls shriveled and peeled back like rice paper, and behind them were the scroll itself and the wooden rods of its mount.
Only then did he understand. He and everything around him were nothing but a few drying drops of ink on some vast, unseen painting. A voice came from beyond the picture, low and even: "That stroke... was unnecessary." And with that, the painter and his room were wiped clean away, leaving behind only a small, unremarkable smudge of ink on the ancient scroll.

小八的涂鸦

讲学已毕，几人正于花田间休息。张万师听到钟声，似有所念。令鸦研墨，在小八的铜钟脑袋上提笔便画。

“这样修改……嗯……还是易切到脑袋……那这样？”
不一会儿，小八的铜钟脑袋上便如刚刚演算用过的稿纸般，如历金戈铁马，一笔一划尽显潦草惨淡。

“师兄！你！你们做什么呢！”
青要夺过张万师的毛笔，却被张万师躲过。
“没算完呢，安静。”

青心中火起，师兄总是如此。若是对常人如此胡来便罢，小八可对自己头上的“症疾”最为敏感。小孩子的心思又最易受伤，这鸦竟也跟着师兄胡来！
只是转头望去，却见小八蹲在水边，不停地摆弄铜脑袋上的图案，心中尽是欢喜。
en:
Xiaoba's doodle

The lecture was over. A few people were resting among the flowers. Zhang Wanshi, hearing the bell, seemed lost in thought. He asked Raven to grind ink, took his brush, and started drawing on Xiaoba's bronze bell head."

Modify it like this... Hmm... Still too easy to cut the head... Then like this?"
In a moment, Xiaoba's bronze bell head was like a draft paper just used for calculations, having endured the metal and fire of battle, every stroke showing desolate hardship.

"Senior Brother! You! What are you doing!"
Halcyon tried to snatch the brush from Zhang Wanshi, but he dodged."
Not done calculating. Quiet."

Halcyon was furious. Senior Brother was always like this. If it were just anyone, fine, but Xiaoba was most sensitive about the "affliction" on his head. A child's heart is most easily hurt. And Raven actually went along with Senior Brother's nonsense!
But looking over, she saw Xiaoba squatting by the water, constantly fiddling with the patterns on his bronze head, his heart full of joy.

zh:
祝英晗这辈子最恼的，就是无端矮人一头。

偏生她上头有个姐姐，虽无血脉之系，却事事都要压过她。
她不服气，总想争一争，旁的且不论，拳脚上总不能输了。
可真动起手来，她反倒被姐姐死死摁在地上，动弹不得。
拳头落下，她不躲。不是躲不开，是不肯。
牙齿咬碎，爬起来，唾一口血沫子，该嘴硬还嘴硬。
姐姐打累了，收了手，她倒追了上去，死命扯住衣角——“凭啥说走就走！”

后来，姐妹俩挑了贼窝，当了山大王，姐姐照样压她一头。
头把交椅是姐姐的，她只得第二把。寨匪们嘴上喊二当家，眼里却只认大当家的面子。她拍桌子瞪眼，压根没人当回事。
好不容易熬到姐姐外出，又来了个狄诚，吊儿郎当往那儿一戳，活像个没脊梁骨的稻草。
可他偏偏能服众，三言两语就打发了那些爱生事的寨匪，寨匪们偏还认这个半路杀出的东西。
她憋了一肚子火，干脆撂下话，往后寨子里不许提“二”字，人人都得喊她大姐头，不然休怪她翻脸不认人。
至于狄诚嘛，她另有一计，既然嘴皮子上赢不过，那便踢花毽，一局定乾坤。

后山空地上，梅花桩林立，狄诚栽楞着倚在上面，望天发呆，浑似个没事人。
“毛丫头，太浮躁，像个飞不高的鸡毛毽，再去练练罢。”
寨匪们听了哄然大笑，浑不把她这个寨主放在眼里。
她攥紧了拳，眉头拧成疙瘩，可蓦地一想，狄诚这话倒也没说错。

小时候她爬桃树，偷摘老头子种的仙桃，一不留神跌下来，正巧摔进了她爹的怀里。
长大后杀进贼窝，贼头子的刀架在脖颈子上，她还没来得及怕，姐姐就一脚飞来，踢得山匪人仰马翻。
再后来接掌山寨，镇不住这班子恶匪，狄诚只消轻飘飘几句话，便能替她挡了灾，解了围。
爹爹爽朗的笑声、姐姐不经意瞥来的目光、狄诚似笑非笑的话头……
它们就像一双手，总能稳稳当当地接住她这只毛躁的毽子。
可她不想被人接着了，她不想做花毽上那根永远短人半截的羽毛，不愿永远停在别人的手掌心里。
她祝英晗不是花毽子，是一团火，火苗蹿起来，是会烧着手的。

开场那日，手下搭了高台，吵嚷不停，锣鼓敲得震天响。
祝英晗手里托着一只花毽子，赤羽如火。
扬手，毽子高高飞起，还没够到头顶的一片云，便坠了下来，直直朝她面门砸去。
“丫头，愣神了！”狄诚的声音比毽子落得还快。
“啰嗦。”
她没有答话，脚尖早已绷紧，铆足了浑身的劲儿，眼睛死死盯着那火红的羽毛——
这一次，她不会再落下。
en:
What irked Zhu Yinghan most in all her life was being made to feel lesser than another without cause.

As fate would have it, she had an elder sister above her. No blood ties between them, yet her sister surpassed her in everything.
She refused to accept it, always itching for a contest. Despite anything else, she could not afford to lose in a fight.
Yet when blows were truly exchanged, she found herself pinned flat to the ground by her sister, unable to move.
The fists came down, and she did not dodge. Not because she could not... she simply would not.
She ground her teeth, hauled herself up, spat a mouthful of bloody froth, and kept her chin high as ever.
When her sister grew tired of it and withdrew, she went after her instead, seizing the hem of her robe with all her might. "What gives you the right to just walk away!"

Later, the two sisters stormed a bandit's den and made themselves rulers of the bandits. Yet still her sister stood above her.
The seat of Chief fell to her sister; she was left with the second. The camp's men called her Second-in-Command on their lips, but in their eyes they acknowledged only the First's authority. She could make all the fuss she liked, and no one would take it to heart.
She had barely endured until her sister departed when along came Di Cheng, slouching there with all the backbone of a straw.
Yet somehow he commanded respect. With a few idle words he got the troublemaking brigands in line, and the men took to this interloper as if he belonged.
She swallowed a belly full of anger and made her declaration: henceforth, no one in the camp was to speak the word "second." Every soul was to call her Big Sister, or they could forget any goodwill from her.
As for Di Cheng, she had another plan. If she could not best him with words, then she would beat him at the Shuttlecock. One match to settle it all.

In the open ground of the Back Mountain, plum blossom stakes stood in rows. Di Cheng leaned against one with a dull expression, gazing vacantly at the sky as though he hadn't a care in the world.
"You are too hasty, lass... like a Shuttlecock that cannot fly high. Go and practice some more."
The bandits burst into laughter at this, paying their own Chief not the slightest regard.
She clenched her fists, her brow knotting tight, yet all at once it struck her that Di Cheng was not entirely wrong.

When she was small, she climbed peach trees to steal the prized fruit the old man grew. Slipped, and tumbled down, falling straight into her father's arms.
When she was grown and stormed the bandit's den, the chief's blade was at her throat. Before she had time to fear, her sister came flying in with a kick that sent the brigand sprawling.
Later, when she took command of the camp and could not hold those wicked men in check, Di Cheng needed only a few airy words to get her out of trouble.
Her father's hearty laughter, the sidelong glance her sister cast without thinking, Di Cheng's half-smiling remarks...
They were like a pair of hands, always there to catch her steady, just like a Shuttlecock.
But she did not wish to be caught. She did not wish to be the feather on the Shuttlecock that was forever shorter than the rest, forever resting in another's palm.
She was no Shuttlecock. She was a fireball, and when its flames leapt up, they would burn the hand that held it.

On the day of the match, her henchmen raised a high platform, the noise and the drums and gongs sounding loud non-stop.
Zhu Yinghan cradled a Shuttlecock in her hand, its feathers red as fire.
She flung it up. The Shuttlecock soared high, but before it reached the cloud above her head, it dropped, falling straight toward her face.
"Lass, you have gone blank!" Di Cheng's voice reached her faster than the Shuttlecock fell.
"Such prattle."
She said nothing more. Her foot was already taut, every last bit of her power coiled and ready, her eyes fixed hard upon those flame-red feathers.
This time, she would not let it fall.

zh:
张错怕黑，至少很早很早之前的时候害怕。黑暗无边无际，既能吞噬一切，又没有尽头，黑暗里能感受到的，只有声音。父亲虚弱的喘息声，有人闯入的破门声，契丹人古怪的喊杀声，一剑一刀的出招声，激烈的争吵声和很久很久的沉默，最后是……什么东西落地的声音。

张错明明什么都不明白，但那一刻，好像懂得了一切。张错知道，他要逃，逃离发生的一切，逃离永不见天日的黑暗，逃离一切。先是在黑暗里跌跌撞撞，摔了腿，再是手脚并用往前爬，折了掌，最后才用肘，挪着一下下往前蹭去。前面隐隐约约传来一个女子的声音，一阵糖油果子的香甜，还隐隐约约透出了——久违的光亮。

眼前的女子青衣红袖，抛下了手中剑刃，先递过来几颗圆滚滚的丹丸，瞧着张错服下，才递过了手中早已凉透的糖油果子。
“有些路，只有亲自走了才懂。阿错，这是你爹教你的最后一课。”
“我姓朱名鱼，从今往后，你便要跟我走了。“
en:
Zhang Cuo was afraid of the dark. At least long ago, he had been. Darkness was endless, boundless. It devoured everything and led nowhere. In the dark, sound is the only thing he can still sense. His father's exhausted breathing. The crash of the door being kicked open. The harsh, alien shouts of Khitan soldiers. The clash of swords and blades. Fierce, desperate arguing. Then a long, long silence. And finally, the dull, heavy thud of something falling to the ground.

Zhang Cuo had understood nothing, and yet somehow, in that moment, he understood everything. He knew he had to run. Run from the ongoing carnage, from the eternal darkness, from everything. He stumbled blindly through the dark, first breaking his leg. Then he crawled on his hands and knees, scratching his palms. In the end, with his elbows, he dragged himself forward inch by inch. He heard a woman's voice just ahead, faint and blurred. He smelled the sweet, lingering scent of candied hawthorn. And beyond it, he saw the faint, long-lost glow of light.

A woman stood there, clad in green with crimson sleeves. She set down her sword, kneeling before him. She offered a few small, round healing pills. Zhang Cuo swallowed them. Then she handed him the candied hawthorn skewer that had long grown cold.

"Some paths," she said, "you have to walk yourself before you can understand. A'Cuo, this is the last lesson your father taught you."

"My name is Zhu Yu," she said, "and from now on, you'll be coming with me."

【泰伯第八】

子曰：“泰伯，其可谓至德也已矣。三以天下让，民无得而称焉。”
子曰：“恭而无礼则劳，慎而无礼则葸，勇而无礼则乱，直而无礼则绞。君子笃于亲，则民兴于仁。 故旧不遗，则民不偷。”
曾子有疾，召门弟子曰：“启予足，启予手。诗云：‘战战兢兢，如临深渊，如履薄冰。’而今而后，吾知免夫！小子！”
曾子有疾，孟敬子问之。曾子言曰：“鸟之将死，其鸣也哀。人之将死，其言也善。君子所贵道者三：动容貌，斯远暴慢矣；正颜色，斯近信矣；出辞气，斯远鄙倍矣。笾豆之事，则有司存。”
曾子曰：“以能问于不能，以多问于寡，有若无，实若虚，犯而不校。昔者吾友尝从事于斯矣。”
曾子曰：“可以托六尺之孤，可以寄百里之命，临大节而不可夺也。君子人与？君子人也。”
曾子曰：“士不可以不弘毅，任重而道远，仁以为己任，不亦重乎？死而后已，不亦远乎？”
子曰：“兴于诗，立于礼，成于乐。”
子曰：“民可使由之，不可使知之。”
子曰：“好勇疾贫，乱也。人而不仁，疾之已甚，乱也。”
子曰：“如有周公之才之美，使骄且悋，其余不足观也已矣。”
子曰：“三年学，不至于谷，不易得也已。”
子曰：“笃信好学，守死善道，危邦不入，乱邦不居。天下有道则见，无道则隐。邦有道，贫且贱焉，耻也。邦无道，富且贵焉，耻也。”
子曰：“不在其位，不谋其政也。”
子曰：“师挚之始，关雎之乱，洋洋乎盈耳哉！”
子曰：“狂而不直，侗而不愿，悾悾而不信，吾不知之矣。”
……
en:
【Tai Bo, Chapter Eight】

The Master said, "Tai Bo may be said to have reached the highest point of virtuous action. Thrice he declined the kingdom, and the people in ignorance of his motives could not express their approbation of his conduct."
The Master said, "Respectfulness, without the rules of propriety, becomes laborious bustle; carefulness, without the rules of propriety, becomes timidity; boldness, without the rules of propriety, becomes insubordination; straightforwardness, without the rules of propriety, becomes rudeness. When those who are in high stations perform well all their duties to their relations, the people are aroused to virtue. When old friends are not neglected by them, the people are preserved from meanness."
The philosopher Zeng being sick, he called to him the disciples of his school, and said, "Uncover my feet, uncover my hands. It is said in the Book of Poetry, 'We should be apprehensive and cautious, as if on the brink of a deep gulf, as if treading on thin ice.' Now and hereafter, I know my escape from all injury to my person, O my children."
The philosopher Zeng being sick, Meng Jing Zi went to ask how he was. Zeng said to him, "When a bird is about to die, its notes are mournful; when a man is about to die, his words are good. There are three principles of conduct which the man of high rank should consider specially important: that in his deportment and manner he keep from violence and heedlessness; that in regulating his countenance he keep near to sincerity; and that in his words and tones he keep far from lowness and impropriety. As to such matters as attending to the sacrificial vessels, there are the proper officers for them."
The philosopher Zeng said, "Gifted with ability, and yet putting questions to those who were not so; possessed of much, and yet putting questions to those possessed of little; having, as though he had not; full, and yet counting himself as empty; offended against, and yet entering into no altercation; formerly I had a friend who pursued this style of conduct."
The philosopher Zeng said, "Suppose that there is an individual who can be entrusted with the charge of a young orphan prince, and can be commissioned with authority over a state of a hundred li, and whom no emergency however great can drive from his principles. Is such a man a superior man? He is a superior man indeed."
The philosopher Zeng said, "The officer may not be without breadth of mind and vigorous endurance. His burden is heavy and his course is long. Perfect virtue is the burden which he considers it is his to sustain; is it not heavy? Only with death does his course stop; is it not long?"
The Master said, "It is by the Odes that the mind is aroused. It is by the Rules of Propriety that the character is established. It is from Music that the finish is received."
The Master said, "The people may be made to follow a path of action, but they may not be made to understand it."
The Master said, "The man who is fond of daring and is dissatisfied with poverty, will proceed to insubordination. So will the man who is not virtuous, when you carry your dislike of him to an extreme."
The Master said, "Though a man have abilities as admirable as those of the Duke of Zhou, yet if he be proud and niggardly, those other things are really not worth being looked at."
The Master said, "It is not easy to find a man who has learned for three years without coming to be good."
The Master said, "With sincere faith he unites the love of learning; holding firm to death, he is perfecting the excellence of his course. Such a one will not enter a tottering state, nor dwell in a disorganized one. When right principles of government prevail in the kingdom, he will show himself; when they are prostrated, he will keep concealed. When a country is well governed, poverty and a mean condition are things to be ashamed of. When a country is ill governed, riches and honor are things to be ashamed of."
The Master said, "He who is not in any particular office has nothing to do with plans for the administration of its duties."
The Master said, "When the music master Zhi first entered on his office, the finish of the Guan Ju was magnificent. How it filled the ears!"
The Master said, "Ardent and yet not upright; stupid and yet not attentive; simple and yet not sincere. Such persons I do not understand."
……

en: The people of the Wuyue Region have always had a deep love for the sea's bounty. History is replete with such tales: Zhuan Zhu offering roasted fish to King Liao of Wu, or the revered Chen Yuanlong and Zhang Jiying, who famously delighted in fresh sashimi. That same devotion endures today. Long before dawn breaks, the rhythmic creak of wooden oars cuts through the morning mist. Soon, a low murmur of voices swells as servants from grand estates and workers from local eateries arrive to claim the day's first catch. Traveling mostly by boat, these familiar patrons bypass the petty haggling over copper coins. Instead, they simply gather their standing orders: fifty sea bass for the wealthy Zhang estate, or three hundred clawed crabs for the Li tavern's signature marinated dishes.

铁锅告诉它，人吃食都丢掉骨头，没有骨头舔，当然不开心啦。
一根筋听完深以为然，第二天出了个大远门，一路挑挑拣拣，终于找到了根最美味的骨头。一根筋一路叼着肉骨头，一路口水滴答流，肚子饿得咕咕叫也不肯啃一口。

en:
His owner is so strange. He can go out and play every day, with plenty of friends, but why is he still hiding and whimpering, or sitting alone and staring into space?
Stubby asks his good friend, a dog named Iron Wok.
Iron Wok explains that humans throw away the bones when they eat, so with no bones to lick, of course, they're unhappy.
This makes perfect sense to Stubby. The next day, he travels far, searching carefully until he finds the most delicious-looking bone. He carries it all the way home, drooling and starving, but never takes a single bite.
Finally home, he places the bone by his owner's bed, hoping that if his owner licks it, the tears will stop.
