en:
An unexpected guest calling himself the Wheat Ridge Recluse sought out Hu Changyi. At that time, Hu was merely a youth, completely unaware of the royal bloodline he carried. The Wheat Ridge Recluse initially intended to reveal Hu's true origins, hoping to use his eloquence to persuade the young man to enter the fray and continue the legacy of the Li-Tang dynasty. However, after spending several days together, he realized that the youth's heart was pure and untainted, holding no attachment whatsoever to the imperial court.

His transcendental heart, free from worldly dust, was in no way inferior to the Recluse's ambition to shape the world. Though the Wheat Ridge Recluse did not achieve his original goal, he accepted the youth as a dear friend despite their age gap, teaching Hu Changyi martial techniques to protect and sustain himself.

To reunite the fragmented realm under heaven, why must one cling to a single dynasty and a single surname? A golden age need not only be resurrected from old soil; it can also be forged upon new ground.

Grand Artisan Su could only sigh. "You greedy creature," he said, "you've just chewed up my next great essay."

zh:
成怀瑾是在平日练习的地儿遇见那游侠的。
那日她正高抬腿跑得起劲，望见官道旁蹲着一人。游侠老远就使劲儿招手，成怀瑾停下来，游侠便凑过来问这问那。哪儿有好玩的？好吃的？走了大半月，净啃干粮了！
你哪来的？清河来的？那咱也是老乡啊！成怀瑾拍拍胸脯，跟我走！
她便带着游侠逛了几日。爬山看海，追着土匪撒丫子跑，日行千里。游侠话是真多啊，讲走过的路、见过的人，高兴处手舞足蹈，失落处也不藏着。成怀瑾也是话不少，她挺喜欢这个风尘仆仆的清河老乡，便什么都讲。她说她做的那些事，不知算不算履历，不知能不能真正帮上人。
游侠听完大叫，算的算的！往日我赶路要自己走，可这回有你带着，轻松多啦！
分别的时候，游侠高兴作揖，说下次还来找她。
成怀瑾站在路口，望着游侠的背影消失在官道尽头，便朝着另一个方向跑去了。那些问题依然困扰着她。无非是因为看不到终点，可看不到又如何？路上还有许多需要她的人的。
人目力有尽，人行却无尽处。不知道去哪时就把腿抬高吧，不断向前走，总会到的。
en:
Cheng Huaijin ran into the wanderer right near her usual training spot.
She was deep into a grueling set of high-knees when she spotted the wanderer squatting by the side of the dirt road, waving frantically at her. The second she stopped, the wanderer hit her with a barrage of questions: Where were the good sights? Where was the good food? The wanderer had been on the road for weeks, gnawing on nothing but stale hardtack!
"Where're you from?" she asked. "Qinghe? No way, that's my hometown!" Huaijin thumped her chest with a grin. "Come with me!"
She spent the next few days playing tour guide. They hiked up mountains, stared out over the ocean, and chased down fleeing bandits, covering miles upon miles every single day. The wanderer was a talker, spinning endless stories about past experiences, throwing their arms around wildly in excitement, and never bothering to hide it when feeling down. Huaijin, being quite the chatterbox herself, found she really liked this dusty wanderer from back home. She eventually confessed her lingering doubts: whether all her random chores actually counted as real experience, and if she was even making a difference.
"It Counts!" The wanderer let out a loud, booming laugh. "It counts! Of course it counts! Normally I have to navigate these miserable roads all by myself, but having you lead the way made this whole trip a breeze!"
When it was finally time to part ways, the wanderer gave her a cheerful, sweeping bow and promised to find her someday in the future.
Huaijin stood at the crossroads, watching the wanderer's silhouette disappear down the long highway. Then, she turned and sprinted off in the opposite direction.
Those heavy questions were still kicking around in the back of her mind, but she realized they only bothered her because she couldn't see the finish line yet. Did that really matter, though? There were still so many people out on the road who needed her help.
Your eyes can only see so far, but your feet can carry you endlessly. When you aren't sure where you're headed, the best thing to do is just drive your knees high. As long as you keep moving forward, you're bound to get there eventually.

他自幼便喜欢看傩戏，他太明白，穿戴上不同的皮相，戏子就成了另一个人。钟馗捉鬼，野狐惑人。覆上面具登了台，人成了角儿，便再不能唱自己的心事。
傩戏看多了，他也就早早悟了个中道理。他不似青妹那般侠心善武，亦没有万师师兄的聪颖天姿，他顶擅长的，就是扮演墨山道最匮缺的那张面目——面上温言软语安抚众心，内里算尽利害护一门周全。自前巨子离世，而师父又猝然故去，山门内外忧患未歇。他从接巨子之位起，便戴上玄铁面具，戴起那张最可靠的面目，此生再未摘下。

而此刻，步入大衍迷阵深处，忽又想起与她初逢那日，他在斩藤时已察觉身后的敌意，回身却见她向自己递来匕首。救鸟之后，她又转身隐入山野，他望着那小小的背影，这是他第一次猜不透一出戏的后续。
后来他明白了，她啊，总是笑骂由心。唯有与她一同度过的时光里，他只是自己。
世间真心难寻，可她对所有人都一样真心……她不知人心至险，桃源尚未能容天下人。她不知人心至险……分明已与他道殊，却还是见他“不经意”露出的染血帕子，便主动提起婚事。

今日，是他第一次在她面前戴上面具，亦是他今生的最后一场戏。
门中有异，穷奇再起。他已无心力再作周旋，却不愿将墨门前路寄于剑走偏锋之人。
他机关算尽，问诛之战，是为她备下的最后一策。

面具坠地，清响如磬。
世间纷扰，再不必算。
恍惚间，他只看见当年两人一道放走的那只鸟，正掠过苍穹。
就让一切向前……鸟儿，飞吧。
en:
Enamored with Nuo opera since childhood, he understood all too well: once a performer dons a different skin, they become someone else entirely. Zhong Kui quells demons; the wild fox beguiles men. Once masked upon the stage, a man becomes a role, and may no longer sing the secrets of his own heart.

Through countless performances, he grasped the truth behind the mask early on. He lacked Halcyon's chivalrous spirit and martial skill, nor did he possess Zhang Wanshi's innate brilliance. His true talent lay in wearing the very face Mohist Hill needed most: soothing the masses with gentle words while calculating every risk and gain, all to shield the sect.

Since the former Grandmaster's passing and his own master's sudden death, strife had never ceased within or beyond the mountain gates. From the moment he ascended as Grandmaster, he donned a mask of black iron, the face of absolute reliability, and never removed it again.

Now, deep within the Evershift Labyrinth, memories of their first meeting surfaced once more. He had already sensed the hostility behind him while cutting through the vines, yet when he turned, he found her holding out a dagger. After saving the bird, she slipped back into the wilds without a word. He watched her small silhouette disappear, and for the first time in his life, he could not predict how the scene would end.

Later, he came to understand: she simply lived as her heart led her, laughing when she felt like laughing, cursing when she felt like cursing. Only in the time they spent together was he ever simply himself.
True hearts are rare in this world, yet she gave hers freely to everyone. She had no idea how treacherous people could be, nor that Haven could never hold all the world within its arms. She had no idea how dangerous it was to trust so openly. And yet, though their paths had long since parted ways, she saw the bloodstained handkerchief he had "accidentally" let slip, and was the one to propose their union.

Today, for the first time, he donned his mask before her. It would be the final performance of his life.
Treachery had taken root within the sect; the Qiongqi Artificers had risen again. He had no strength left for more maneuvering, but he refused to hand the future of the Mohists to someone who would win by reckless extremes. He had weighed every gain and loss, and what came next was the last plan he could leave her.

The mask hit the ground with a clear, bell-like ring. At last, there was nothing left to calculate.

In the blur of it all, he saw only the bird they had set free together, cutting across the sky.

Let everything move forward.

Fly, little bird. Fly.

zh:
话说这陈子奚刚与江晏相识不久，便发现他总在读一本书。江晏白天读、晚上读、喝酒时读、得空便读。陈子奚以为江晏这般专注是在看什么江湖逸事。而如此好物他竟也不主动与自己分享，大约是没把自己当朋友，实在可恶。
是以陈子奚只得主动开口向江晏索要。

“门派之物，不可外传。”江无浪回绝得倒是干净，却惹得陈子奚更加好奇。莫不是什么门派秘辛，还不可与外人说道？
抓心挠肝的滋味忒不好受。陈子奚只得趁江晏熟睡，从包裹中将书偷拿过来翻阅。此书没有标题，看着陈旧倒也平平无奇。可才翻开看了一页，陈子奚便愣在当场。这书上密密麻麻写的全是刀法招式。原来，让江无浪日夜不眠、茶饭不思的竟是……一本刀法。真不知该说此人有趣还是无趣。

隔日清晨，江无浪复又翻开他那本刀法准备研习，却看到里面不知何时多了一些批注。
“批：如此晦涩难懂，你们门派莫不是天书派？”
“批：此书即便外传，也不会有人感兴趣的。你可放心了……”
“批：我都看完了，确实看不懂，不必再往下看了。”
“批：喝酒去吗，江晏？”
江无浪皱起了眉头，抬眼看向陈子奚。
只见陈摇了摇扇子笑问：喝酒去吗，江晏？
en:
Shortly after meeting Jiang Yan, Chen Zixi noticed his constant reading. Day and night. While drinking. Every spare moment. Assuming it must be thrilling martial arts tales, Chen grew offended. Keeping such entertainment to himself meant Jiang Yan didn't consider them friends! The outrage! Thus, Chen had no choice but to demand a look.

"Sect secrets are not for outsiders." Jiang's refusal was firm, which only made Zixi more curious. Was it some scandalous sect history? Forbidden knowledge? The itch of not knowing was unbearable. So when Yan was asleep, Zixi stole the book from his pack. No title. Worn cover. Utterly unremarkable. Then he opened it. Page after page of densely packed blade techniques. This was what had Jiang so obsessed? A manual of blade skills? The man was either fascinating or painfully dull.

The next morning, Jiang opened his book to find new annotations:
"Note: Are you sure it's not 'Book of Heaven'? This is incomprehensible."
"Note: Even if you shared this, no one would care. Rest easy."
"Note: I finished it. Still don't understand. No need to keep reading."
"Note: Drinks, Jiang Yan?"

Jiang frowned and looked up at Chen. Zixi fanned himself lazily.

"Drinks, Jiang Yan?"

zh:
陈宅今日格外热闹。仆人进进出出，打包各类物什。从里外衣物到不同料子的酒盏，一件件妥当收好，酒盏用细麻布裹严缠紧，小心摞进木箱，搬进马车。如今不比以前拎着个小包裹就能上路的时候了。总管安叔站在院里，有条不紊地指挥众人。
这场忙碌的源头也掺和在人堆里东摸摸西看看。一会儿拿折扇指指点点：“老安，我走了以后，记得给松树剪枝啊。”一会儿又眼疾手快，从路过侍女端着的点心盒里顺走一块定胜糕，丢进嘴里。
搬着箱子的绿衣管家从他身边路过，头也没抬：“你要实在没事干，也可以一起来收拾。”
另一个小小脑袋钻进他们中间。眉心一点红的小孩绷着脸，严肃地指正：“师父身体不好，不可受累。”
陈子奚煞有介事地点头附和：“对，不可受累。”
安叔也不吭声，脚下一拐，把手里箱子直接塞进陈慎怀里：“那少主受累，搬出去吧。”
“哦。”小孩乖乖接过来，抱着箱子往外走，哼哧哼哧。

陈子奚在后头看得直笑。安叔核对着手里要收拾物件的单子，冷不丁开口：“突然说要跑那么大老远去接人——是你总念叨的那个当年救下来的小孩吧。”
陈子奚愣了一下，旋即笑起来：“是啊是啊。那小孩可好玩了，我说什么都信，最是买账。”
“那带回来之后，准备干什么？”
“不干什么啊。”陈子奚说，“游一游杭州，看一看风光。小慎每天背医书也辛苦，正好跟小慎一起找找乐子。要么，找找小慎的乐子也行。”
安叔看了他一会儿，微微低下头，声音沉下来：“没别的意思，只是如果你想做什么，跟家里人说一声。我们好早做准备。”

陈子奚慢慢收起了笑脸，手指在扇骨上轻轻敲了两下。笃，笃。
“我要的就是不干什么。不要猜我说的话。”

他声音不大。院子里安静下来。西湖的风吹进来，院中青松轻摇，拨动微小的松涛。周遭只剩下外头仆人搬运东西走动的细碎声响。
深绿衣衫的管家没再说话，鞠了一躬，准备转身离开。这时候陈子奚忽然又笑了起来。他摸了摸下巴：“要么，送孩子去读书？平澜书院就很不错啊。”
en:
The Chen Manor was unusually busy today. Servants hurried in and out, packing everything from underclothes and outer robes to wine cups of every material. Each cup was wrapped snugly in fine hemp cloth, carefully stacked in a wooden chest, and carried out to the carriage. Gone were the days when a small bundle was all anyone needed for a journey. Uncle An, the head steward, stood in the courtyard, calmly directing the preparations.
The man responsible for all this bustle was in the thick of it, poking about and inspecting whatever caught his eye. One moment, he was gesturing with his folding fan. "An, don't forget to prune the pines while I'm away." The next, he had snatched a cake from a passing maid's pastry box and popped it into his mouth.
The green-robed steward walked past with a chest in his arms. Without looking up, he said, "If you're so short of things to do, you could help us pack."
A small head pushed between them. The child with the red dot between his brows looked utterly serious. "Master isn't well. He mustn't tire himself out."
Chen Zixi nodded solemnly. "Quite right. Mustn't tire myself out."
Uncle An said nothing. He simply changed direction and deposited the chest in Chen Shen's arms. "Then perhaps our young master can carry this outside."
"Oh. Alright." The boy obediently took the chest and staggered away, huffing with effort.

Chen Zixi watched him go, laughing. Uncle An consulted his packing list, then spoke without looking up. "This sudden journey to fetch someone from so far away... It's that child you rescued, isn't it? The one you're always talking about."
Chen Zixi paused, then grinned. "Yes, that's the one. Such fun. Believes every word I say. Always gives me a good audience."
"And what do you plan to do once you've brought the child back?"
"Nothing in particular," said Chen Zixi. "Show the child around Hangzhou. Take in the sights. Shen spends all day memorizing medical texts. They could have some fun together. Or they could have some fun at Shen's expense. That works too."
Uncle An studied him for a moment, then lowered his head a little. His voice grew quiet. "I don't mean to pry. But if you're planning something, tell the household. Give us time to prepare."

Chen Zixi's smile slowly faded. He tapped a finger twice against the ribs of his fan. Tap. Tap.
"I mean to do nothing. Don't look for hidden meanings in what I say."

He hadn't raised his voice. The courtyard fell silent. A breeze from West Lake stirred the pines, their needles rustling softly. Beyond the courtyard, servants' footsteps and the faint sounds of packing carried on.
The steward in dark green bowed without another word and turned to leave. Then Chen Zixi smiled again, rubbing his chin. "Or perhaps I should send the child to school? Pinglan Academy is rather good."

zh: 南朝宋刘义庆招聚文学之士，采摭汉末至东晋名士轶闻逸事，依德行、言语、政事、文学、方正、雅量等三十六门，著为《世说新语》。《隋书·经籍志》著录于子部小说家类，称《世说》，凡八卷；《旧唐书·经籍志》亦入小说家，题《世说》十卷。其书辞约旨远，善以寥寥数语传人物之神采，摹清谈之风度，故后世多归之子部小说家，以为志人笔记之祖。然其中所记名士品藻、任诞、栖逸、贤媛诸事，亦足补史传之阙，观魏晋士族之习尚、门阀之兴衰，不可无此编也。虽为小说家言，然风流隽永，后世诗文用典取象，多出其中。
en: Liu Yiqing of the Liu Song dynasty in the Southern Courts gathered about him scholars of letters and collected the anecdotes and stray tales of eminent men from the close of the Han through to the Eastern Jin, arranging them under thirty-six categories—among them Virtuous Conduct, Speech, Governance, Letters, Square Integrity, and Elegant Breadth of Mind—and composed therewith New Accounts of the World. The Book of Sui: Treatise on Classics counted under the fiction category of the philosophers' section, calling it the Accounts of the World in eight volumes; the Old Book of Tang: Treatise on Classics likewise placed it among the fiction category, listing the Accounts of the World in ten volumes. Terse in its phrasing yet far-reaching in its meaning, the work excels at rendering the spirit of its characters in a handful of words, and capturing the manner of the pure conversation of the age. And so later ages have chiefly placed it among the fiction writers of the philosophers' section, regarding it as the forefather of character sketches and jottings. Yet the accounts within it of eminent men's discernment, their unrestrained ways, their retreats from the world, and the virtuous women among them are equally sufficient to supply what is wanting in the formal histories. And for observing the customs of the gentry of Wei and Jin and the rise and fall of the great clans, this work is indispensable. Though it be counted among the fiction writers, it is romantic and enduring in its grace, and later poets and writers drew their allusions and imagery from it more than from almost any other source.

zh: 执行德不能发扬光大，信仰道不忠实坚定，（这样的人）有他不为多，没他不为少。1992年出土于敦煌悬泉置遗址。木简1枚，松木。简长13、宽0.8厘米。传世本文献中此两段文字为：“子张曰：‘执德不弘，信道不笃，焉能为有，焉能为亡？’子夏之门人，问交于子张。子张曰：‘子夏云何？’对曰：‘子夏曰：可者与之，其不可者拒之。’子张曰：‘异乎吾所闻。君子尊贤而容众，嘉善而矜不能。我之大贤与，于人何所不容；我之不贤与，人将拒我，如之何其拒人也？’”简上文字与传世本《论语》的文字略有小异，在版本学和校勘学上有一定价值。另外，《论语》残文的发现，为研究儒家学说在河西的传播提供了重要依据。
en: If a man holds to virtue but does not broaden it, and if he believes in the Way but is not steadfast in it, what does it matter if he exists or not? Discovered in 1992 at the Dunhuang Celestial Spring Site, this pine wood slip measures 13 centimeters long and 0.8 centimeters wide. It records a philosophical dialogue from the Analects concerning virtue and friendship: "Zizhang said: 'If a man holds to virtue but does not broaden it, and if he believes in the Way but is not steadfast, what does it matter if he exists or not?' The disciples of Zixia asked Zizhang about friendship. Zizhang asked them, 'What does Zixia teach?' They replied, 'Zixia says: Associate with those who are worthy, and reject those who are not.' Zizhang responded, 'This differs from what I have been taught. A gentleman honors the worthy but is tolerant of the masses. He praises the good but has compassion for the incompetent. If I am truly a man of great virtue, whom among men can I not tolerate? If I am lacking in virtue, others will reject me, so how could I possibly be in a position to reject them?'" Since the text on this slip differs slightly from the standard, traditionally transmitted versions of the classic, it is highly valued by historians for textual criticism and manuscript comparison. Furthermore, finding this fragment on the remote northwestern frontier provides crucial evidence of how widely Confucian thought had spread through the Hexi Corridor during ancient times.

en:
East of the Qinghe's farthest reaches lie ruins that stretch for miles. This was once the former territory of the Northern Vow from the previous dynasty. In those days, when the Khitan invaded the Middle Kingdom, the Northern Vow retreated to Qinghe. From this fortified city, they resisted the Khitan iron cavalry for several months. Regrettably, the city ultimately fell and its people perished, resulting in devastating losses for both sides. Afterward, they engaged in guerrilla warfare throughout the Qinghe region, finally forcing the Khitan invaders to retreat from the Central Plains.
Old tales tell that the warriors of the Northern Vow once swore the Yanyun Oath: "I vow to protect this land with my life." Now, gazing upon these ruined cities and wild lands, how deeply it stirs the heart with solemn awe.

en:
Tiger General is a very, very old cat now. His eyes are clouded with age, and even jumping onto the lowest haystack leaves him panting for a long while.
But once... once, he was something else. At Hai Hour, he would sharpen his claws on the Grain Storehouse. At Zi Hour, he would patrol the rafters, a tiger ready to pounce at the slightest sound. At Chen Hour, he would collect fresh fish from his bowl, then nap on the highest haystack.
He remembers now... There was a person, once.
That person would hold him and say, "Thank you, Tiger General. When the grain piles up to the beams, the mountain will open."
Seasons passed. New wheat in the jars became old wheat. Squeak, squeak, those wretched mice were back. He flicked his tail weakly, stirring only dust. He was too old to catch mice now.
Why hadn't that person come back?

zh:
十五六岁的刘娴瘦得像个皮包骨，骨头都戳人。
人也一样，那些和她一道做工的人都这样说，看起来脸上有点笑模样，但手头半点儿不帮人的，不是自己的活，碰都不会碰上一点儿！脾气还臭的很，像是怕谁都要欺负她似的，还有、还有倒是成日巴结工头。
议论了一阵子，他们又说，她不是没地方去吗，不这样干哪儿给她活路，都是可怜人，这年头只有那些大老爷活得好。
说完这一通之后，围在一道的人又都散了。

因为她是这样的人，所以他们说的是“像是怕谁欺负她似的”。
如果她不是这样的人，他们说的会是“活该受人欺负”。
她要前一个，也不要后一个，后一个她试过了，太疼，会哭。

后来，日子久了，多打了几个照面，这些说闲话的人也打听起她的事来，咬着馍馍问她。
“你爹呢。”
“跑了。”
“你娘呢。”
“死了。”
她这话说得果断，以至于听的人发愣，那些同情和怜悯都配不上她口中的利落。
“死得早，我记不得了。”
每次说完这句话之后，他们眼中会有明白了，怪不得的样子。
而在这些瞬间，她又会想起那个晚上，她唯一记得的那一小段——
快要死的女人一辈子没对她好过，此刻却盯着她哭，口中咿咿呀呀地说话，刘娴一句也听不清，茫然地看向那两片像是死鱼一样张合，却碰不上的唇瓣。
她死死地拽着刘娴的手，彻底不动了。最后，刘娴摸了摸那张皮包着骨头的脸，在干涸的生命上，只摸到眼眶吐出的最后一片潮湿，她为什么要哭呢，死一定很疼，所以才会哭。
en:
Fifteen or sixteen-year-old Liu Xian was so thin she was practically skin and bones, the kind that poked at you. 
And so was her personality, or so said the women who worked alongside her. "She might smile a little, but she won't lift a finger to help anyone. Won't touch work that isn't hers! And what a temper, like she's afraid everyone's out to get her. Oh, and don't forget how she's always sucking up to the foreman."
After muttering among themselves, they'd add: "Well, it's not like she's got anywhere else to go. What choice does she have? These days, only the rich live well." 
And with that, the huddle would disperse. 

Because she was like this, they said, "She's afraid everyone's out to get her." 
If she weren't, they'd say, "Serves her right if people bully her." 
She'd take the first over the second. She'd tried the second before. It hurt too much. It made her cry. 

Later, as time passed and they crossed paths more, the gossipers started asking her questions directly as they chewed on their steamed buns. 
"Where's your father?" 
"Ran off." 
"Your mother?" 
"Dead." 
She said it so sharply that it left them stunned, their pity unable to keep up with her bluntness. 
"Died early. I don't remember her." Every time she said this, their eyes would flicker with understanding. Ah, no wonder. 
And in those moments, she'd remember that night, the only fragment she could recall...
The woman who'd never been kind to her stared at her weeping, babbling incoherently. Liu Xian couldn't understand a word, just watched her fish-like lips open and close without sound. 
She clutched Liu Xian's hand until her grip went limp. Finally, Liu Xian touched that gaunt face and felt only a single damp trail from her eye. A final tear. Why cry? she wondered. Death must hurt.

Since the Khitan blocked the grain routes, the surrounding area has no longer been peaceful. Sentinel not only stands guard at the gate with the soldiers by day but also sacrifices his rest at night to monitor any movement nearby. Several times, night raids on the Toilgrain Barn conducted by Khitan soldiers were thwarted thanks to Sentinel's alertness.

zh: 《周礼》成于战国至汉初，汇集了先秦官制与理想政典。原名《周官》，亦称《周官经》，汉刘歆校理秘府藏书时更名为《周礼》。全书分天官冢宰、地官司徒、春官宗伯、夏官司马、秋官司寇、冬官司空六篇，六官之下各有属官，职掌分明，体大思精，所涉吏治、赋税、礼乐、兵刑、营造诸事，兼及教育、科技等领域，是中国古代第一部系统叙述官制的专书。西汉时《冬官》散佚，汉儒取《考工记》补之，记百工技艺之事。汉代立于学官，列于三礼。相传为周公所作，然其官制与西周典制多有不合，东汉何休等已有“六国阴谋之书”之疑。东汉郑玄遍注群经，以《周礼》为“周公致太平之迹”，作《周官礼注》，《周礼》遂跃居三礼之首。唐贾公彦据郑注作疏，孔颖达等奉诏修定，遂为官学取士之本。
en: Rites of Zhou was compiled between the Warring States period and the early Han dynasty, bringing together the official institutions and ideal political canons of the pre-Qin era. Originally titled the Offices of Zhou, and also known as the Canon of the Offices of Zhou, it was renamed Rites of Zhou by the Han scholar Liu Xin when he catalogued the hidden archives of the imperial library. The full work is divided into six chapters: the Heavenly Office of the Chief Minister, the Earthly Office of the Minister of Multitudes, the Spring Office of the Grand Ritualist, the Summer Office of the Minister of War, the Autumn Office of the Minister of Justice, and the Winter Office of the Minister of Works, each with its subordinate offices, their duties clearly delineated. Vast in size and meticulous in thought, the work encompasses subjects such as civil administration, taxation, ritual and music, military and penal affairs, and construction, extending also into the domains of education and techniques. It is the first work in Chinese antiquity to offer a systematic account of official institutions. During the Western Han, the Winter Office chapter was lost; Han Confucians supplemented it with the Record of Crafts, which records the Techniques of the Artisans. It was enshrined among the official academies in the Han dynasty and listed among the Three Rites. It is said to have been composed by the Duke of Zhou, yet its institutional arrangements depart considerably from the canonical institutions of the Western Zhou. As early as the Eastern Han, He Xiu and others had voiced suspicion that it was "a book of stratagems from the Six States." The Eastern Han scholar Zheng Xuan, who composed commentaries on the full canon of classics, regarded the Rites of Zhou as "the traces of the Duke of Zhou's achievement of great peace" and wrote the Annotations on the Rites of the Offices of Zhou, whereupon the Rites of Zhou rose to stand foremost among the Three Rites. In the Tang, Jia Gongyan composed a subcommentary based on Zheng Xuan's annotations, and Kong Yingda and others revised it by imperial decree, establishing it as the foundation for the official examinations.
Above all, guard the flame in your hand.

显德五年三月，敕命翰林学士都承旨陶谷、司天监赵修巳赐王犒军帛三万匹，并羊马橐驼。每岁班赐自此始。

秋八月，敕遣阁门使曹彬赐王马军钢甲二百、步军甲五千，并兵器、旗帜等。
九月，敕遣使赐王羊五千口、马二百匹、橐二十头。
显德六年夏四月，敕升湖州为宣德军，授王兄弘偡特进、检校太尉，充本军节度使。
六月，赐两浙进贡使钱三千贯、绢五千匹、银器三千两。

建隆元年夏四月，敕授王天下兵马大元帅，加食邑千户，实封五百户。

建隆二年三月，敕遣使丁德裕送王弟弘信回，仍赐王战马二百匹、羊五百口、驼二十头。
建隆三年，春二月，敕遣右殿直王蓍来宣谕，仍赐国信。
夏五月，东阳、信安、新定三郡民灾，王遣使赈恤。
冬十月，敕遣上殿直景德伦授两镇节度，王世子惟濬为邕州建武军节度使。
建隆四年正月，敕遣使赐王马、驼、羊等。
冬十月，敕遣引进使丁德裕来宣谕，仍加王食邑一千户，实封四百户，改赐承家保国宣德守道忠贞恭顺功臣，又加建武军节度使、王世子惟濬检校太尉。

en:
In the second year of Qianyou, in the tenth month of winter, an imperial edict dispatched the Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Zhang Xu and others, bearing credentials and full ceremonial rites, to invest the Prince as King of Wuyue, and further bestowed upon him a jade tablet, a golden seal, and ceremonial regalia.
In the eleventh month, the Grand Lady Shunde of the Wuyue Kingdom was invested.
In the autumn of the first year of Xiande, the seventh month, an imperial edict dispatched an envoy to further confer upon the King the title "Supreme Marshal of All Armies Under Heaven," and bestowed upon him a golden seal.
In the second month of the third year of Xiande, an imperial edict dispatched the Palace Attendant Xue Youguang to proclaim the decree, and further bestowed ceremonial robes, headwear, and regalia to be worn upon the body.
In the eighth month of the fourth year of Xiande, an imperial edict dispatched the Remonstrance Doctor Yin Richeng, bestowing upon the King, for his birthday, two sets of crimson imperial robes.
In the third month of the fifth year of Xiande, an imperial edict commanded the Hanlin Academician and Deputy Chief Herald Tao Gu, together with Zhao Xiusi of the Imperial Observatory, to bestow upon the King thirty thousand bolts of silk to reward his troops, along with sheep, horses, and camels. The yearly bestowal of gifts began from this time onward.
In the summer, the fourth month, an imperial edict dispatched Zhou Guang, Chief of All Armies Under Heaven, to proclaim the decree, and further bestowed garments upon Shao Keqian and others, and upon the officers and soldiers, in varying measure.
In the autumn, the eighth month, an imperial edict dispatched the Gate Commissioner Cao Bin to bestow upon the King two hundred sets of steel armor for the cavalry, five thousand sets of armor for the infantry, along with weapons and banners.
In the ninth month, an imperial edict dispatched an envoy to bestow upon the King five thousand sheep, two hundred horses, and twenty camels.
In the summer of the sixth year of Xiande, the fourth month, an imperial edict elevated Huzhou to Xuande Military Prefecture, and conferred upon the King's elder brother Hongyan the titles of Specially Advanced and Inspector Grand Commandant, to serve as Military Governor of the prefecture.
In the sixth month, the tribute envoy of the Two Zhe regions was bestowed three thousand strings of coin, five thousand bolts of silk, and three thousand liang of silver vessels.
In the autumn, the eighth month, an edict increased the King's fief by one thousand households, with four hundred households in actual enfeoffment, and further bestowed the honorific title of Meritorious Minister for Upholding Benevolence, Illuminating Virtue, Proclaiming Loyalty, Preserving Blessings, Supporting Heaven, and Aiding Brightness. The King's principal consort, Lady Sun, was also invested as the Virtuous Lady of the Wuyue Kingdom, and the King's heir apparent, Weijun, was appointed Deputy Military Governor of Zhenhai and Zhendong, and Inspector Grand Guardian.
In the summer of the first year of Jianlong, the fourth month, an edict conferred upon the King the title of Grand Marshal of All Armies Under Heaven, increasing his fief by one thousand households, with five hundred households in actual enfeoffment.
In the sixth month, an edict further conferred upon the Virtuous Lady of Wuyue Kingdom, Lady Wu, the title of Virtuous and Serene Lady. The King's heir apparent Weijun, Deputy Military Governor of the Two Armies, was also granted the titles of Golden and Purple Grand Master for Splendid Happiness and Inspector Grand Guardian, and made Military Governor. An edict further elevated Mingzhou to Fengguo Military Prefecture, and conferred upon the King's younger brother Hongyi the titles of Golden and Purple Grand Master for Splendid Happiness and Inspector Grand Guardian, to serve as Military Governor of the prefecture.
In the winter, the eleventh month, Yangzhou was pacified, and an edict dispatched the Messenger of Communications Wang Jiyun and Ding Deyu to proclaim the decree, and further bestowed a "Token of State Trust."
In the third month of the second year of Jianlong, an edict dispatched the envoy Ding Deyu to escort the King's younger brother Hongxin back, and further bestowed upon the King two hundred warhorses, five hundred sheep, and twenty camels.
In the spring of the third year of Jianlong, the second month, an edict dispatched the Right Palace Attendant Wang Shi to proclaim the decree, and further bestowed a Token of State Trust.
In the summer, the fifth month, the three prefectures of Dongyang, Xin'an, and Xinding suffered calamity among the people, and the King dispatched envoys to grant relief.
In the winter, the tenth month, an edict dispatched the Upper Palace Attendant Jing Delun to confer governorship of two garrisons, and the King's heir apparent Weijun was made Military Governor of Jianwu Prefecture in Yongzhou.
In the first month of the fourth year of Jianlong, an edict dispatched an envoy to bestow upon the King horses, camels, sheep, and other gifts.
In the winter, the tenth month, an edict dispatched the Introduction Commissioner Ding Deyu to proclaim the decree, further increasing the King's fief by one thousand households, with four hundred households in actual enfeoffment, and bestowing the new honorific title of Meritorious Minister for Upholding the Family, Preserving the State, Proclaiming Virtue, Guarding the Way, and Loyal Submission, and further conferring upon the King's heir apparent Weijun, Military Governor of Jianwu Prefecture, the title of Inspector Grand Commandant.

它们有的泛着蜜蜡般的暖黄，有的缀着翡翠似的青绿。
它们晶莹剔透，干净得就像那些匠人们的心。
en:
Mysterious ore, usable as a material.

Found on precipitous cliffs, these ores were only revealed to the world through the mining efforts of the artisans in the Mirkvale.
Some glow with a warm honey-yellow, while others are speckled with an emerald green.
They are crystal clear and as pure as the hearts of the artisans.
